sens: Prince of the tribe of Naphtali
H6300.detail: Pedahel is a tribal leader mentioned only once in the Bible. His name means "redeemed by God" or "delivered by God." He is presented in Numbers 34:28 as the designated prince to represent the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the lands of Canaan after the conquest.
H6300.origine: The name Pedahel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "pedah" which means "to redeem, to rescue, to deliver" (also found in the name Pedaiah), and "El" which designates God. It is therefore a theophoric name, meaning it invokes the name of God. This type of name expresses God's action on behalf of a person or family.
H6300.emploi: Pedahel appears only once in the Scriptures, in Numbers 34:28. He is mentioned in the context of the division of the promised land: Moses designates the leaders of the twelve tribes who will oversee the allocation of the lands of Canaan among the families of Israel. Pedahel, son of Ammihud, represents the tribe of Naphtali in this crucial role of territorial administration.

sens: Father of Gamaliel, chief of the tribe of Manasseh at the Exodus
H6301.detail: Pedahtsur is a man from the time of the Exodus, whose name means "the Rock has redeemed." He is known only as the father of Gamaliel, who was designated as chief (prince) of the tribe of Manasseh during the census of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 1:10). Gamaliel represented his tribe in the organization of the camp, the presentation of the consecration offerings, and the march of the people through the wilderness (Numbers 2:20; 7:54-59; 10:23).
H6301.origine: The name Pedahtsur is composed of two Hebrew words: "pedah," which means "ransom" or "redemption," and "tsur," which means "rock" or "stone." The imagery evokes trust in God as an unchanging rock and savior. This type of theophoric name (which contains the name of God) was common among the Israelites and expressed a religious conviction: the Rock (God) brings salvation and protection.
H6301.emploi: Pedahtsur appears only five times in the Bible, always in the book of Numbers, and each time in connection with his son Gamaliel. The first occurrence (Numbers 1:10) introduces him during the first census of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. The subsequent occurrences mention him again in relation to Gamaliel: during the ordered camp (Numbers 2:20), at the presentation of the offerings of the tribal leaders (Numbers 7:54-59), and in the counting of the military units that set out (Numbers 10:23). Pedahtsur himself plays no active role: he is mentioned only to identify his son.

sens: Chief of a family of temple servants during the exile and return
H6303.detail: Padon is a proper name designating a man who lived during the time of the exile in Babylon and the return to the promised land. He is mentioned as the chief or ancestor of a family of servants attached to the temple (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47). These lists enumerate the families of temple servants who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel to rebuild worship in Jerusalem.
H6303.origine: The name Padon literally means "ransom" or "the one who redeems" in Hebrew. It is a meaningful name that evokes the idea of deliverance or liberation, which is fitting for a man whose descendants returned from Babylonian captivity. The name perhaps underscores the central theme of exile: the ransom and restoration of God's people.
H6303.emploi: Padon appears twice in Scripture, always in the lists of families of temple servants who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from exile in Babylon. He is cited in Ezra 2:44, in the account of the people's return and the reconstruction of the temple, and again in Nehemiah 7:47, where the same list is repeated. These two parallel passages attest to the importance of preserving the memory of the descendants of the temple servants, guardians of the cultic continuity after the captivity.

sens: Action of saving, delivering someone from servitude or misfortune
Payment of a ransom to free a captive or a slave
Liberation of God's people by His grace and power
Marked and miraculous separation or distinction
H6304.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of saving, delivering someone from a situation of slavery or misfortune. It is a powerful intervention that liberates: in Psalms 130:7, one puts their hope in God because "redemption is with Him in abundance," meaning that God has the power and will to save His people.
2. Originally, the word evokes the payment of a ransom to free a captive or a slave: one "redeems" their freedom by paying a price. In Isaiah 50:2, God asks: "Is my hand too short to redeem?" — referring to His ability to free Israel from danger.
3. In the history of Israel, redemption is primarily the work of God who delivers His people: in Psalms 111:9, "He has sent redemption to His people," it is God who sovereignly acts to save.
4. The word can also signify a marked distinction or separation: in Exodus 8:19, God says, "I will make a distinction between my people and your people," showing His miraculous protection for Israel.
H6304.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to pay a price" or "to redeem." It is linked to the economic idea of redemption: when one pays to free someone, they "redeem" them. This notion extends to theological language to speak of the liberation that God performs for His people — not because He pays a ransom to someone else, but because He exercises His power to free His own from evil and slavery.
H6304.emploi: The word appears four times in the Segond, with nuances depending on the context. In Exodus 8:19, it denotes a distinction or separation between God's people and others. In Psalms 111:9 and 130:7, it takes on its full meaning: the deliverance that God brings to Israel, His gracious salvation. In Isaiah 50:2, it is God's action that "redeems" or saves His people from captivity or misfortune. The term always evokes God's intervention, never a human action: it is His work of liberation.
H6304.portee: This word reminds us that salvation is not a commercial transaction: God does not pay a ransom to a third party, but He exercises His sovereign power to free His people from evil. For the Christian, redemption speaks of the deliverance that God alone can offer, by grace and not by merit. It invites one to place their hope in God alone, for it is He who "redeems" and saves.

sens: Father of Zebidda, wife of King Josiah and mother of King Jehoiakim of Judah
Father of Zerubbabel and brother of Shealtiel
H6305G.detail:
1. Pedajah is a man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the father of Zebidda, the wife of King Josiah of Judah and mother of King Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:36). His name appears only once in the Bible, in the account of Jehoiakim's accession to the throne.
2. Pedajah is also mentioned as the father of Zerubbabel and brother of Shealtiel. Shealtiel is usually called the father of Zerubbabel, likely due to the lack of a direct heir in his lineage, but Pedajah is the true father according to transmitted traditions.
H6305G.origine: The name Pedajah means "Jehovah has redeemed" or "God has redeemed." It is composed of the divine element Yah (God) and the verb "to redeem," thus expressing a salvific action of God towards His people.
H6305G.emploi: Pedajah appears explicitly mentioned only once in the biblical text: in 2 Kings 23:36, where he is named as the father of Zebidda, the mother of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He should also be distinguished from Pedajah, the father of Zerubbabel, an important figure at the time of the return from Babylonian exile, although the latter is not named in the text provided here. This man belongs to the class of notables of the kingdom of Judah before its fall.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Father of Zerubbabel and brother of Shealtiel
H6305H.detail:
1. Pedajah is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned during the time when the kingdom was divided between the north and the south. He belongs to the royal lineage of Judah and appears in the genealogy of the kings (1 Chronicles 3:18).
2. Pedajah is the father of Zerubbabel and the brother of Shealtiel. Although Shealtiel is often called the father of Zerubbabel, Pedajah is his biological father (1 Chronicles 3:19). Zerubbabel became the governor of Judah during the return from Babylonian exile and played a major role in the reconstruction of the temple.
H6305H.origine: The name Pedajah means "Jehovah has redeemed." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (Jehovah) and a root evoking redemption. This name expresses trust in divine deliverance, characteristic of the theophoric names of this royal period.
H6305H.emploi: Pedajah is mentioned twice in the Scriptures, both in 1 Chronicles 3. First as the son of Shealtiel and brother of Malkiram, Shenahtsar, Jekamia, Hoshama, and Nedabiah (1 Chronicles 3:18). Then as the father of Zerubbabel and of Shimei (1 Chronicles 3:19). These mentions place Pedajah in the succession of Jehoiachin after the Babylonian exile, at a pivotal time when the existence of the Jewish people was threatened but where God maintained His dynastic promise.
H6305H.portee: Pedajah's role in the genealogy shows how God preserved the royal lineage of Judah up to Zerubbabel, who brought the captive people back to Jerusalem. His very existence testifies to God's faithfulness to His promises, even in the darkest hours of exile.

sens: Man of the kingdom of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H6305I.detail: Pedajah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:20, where he is presented as the father of Joel, who served as chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh under King David.
H6305I.origine: The name Pedajah means "The Lord has redeemed" or "The Lord has freed," formed from Hebrew roots meaning "ransom" or "liberation" and "the Lord." It is a theophoric name, that is, a name that includes the divine name, expressing the belief that God had redeemed or freed the bearer. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, reflecting the common faith in God's liberating action.
H6305I.emploi: Pedajah appears in 1 Chronicles 27:20 as the father of Joel who managed the affairs of the half-tribe of Manasseh during King David's reign. Although mentioned only once in this administrative context, the name appears elsewhere in the Old Testament to designate other individuals, notably a man related to Zerubbabel, but the Bible provides no further details about his life or deeds here.

sens: Man of Judah during the time of exile and return
H6305J.detail: Pedajah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He was the son of Pareosh and participated in the restoration work of the walls, as a worker responsible for a specific section (Nehemiah 3:25).
H6305J.origine: The name Pedajah means "Jehovah has redeemed" or "God has redeemed." It is composed of two elements: "peda" (ransom, deliverance) and "Yah" (Jehovah). This name reflects trust in divine redemption.
H6305J.emploi: Pedajah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:25, as one of the workers who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, after the return from Babylonian exile. He was the son of Pareosh and was entrusted with the responsibility of fortifying a section of the walls near the royal prison courtyard.

sens: Man who stood beside the scribe Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H6305K.detail: 1. Pedaja is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during a solemn scene where the scribe Ezra reads the Law to the people at the time of the Return from Exile. He stands to the left of Ezra on the platform, alongside other important men (Nehemiah 8:4). His exact role is not specified, but his presence among these prominent figures suggests that he was a respected and influential personality in the reconstituted community.
H6305K.origine: The name Pedaja literally means "God has redeemed" or "the Lord has redeemed," formed from two Hebrew elements: פְּדָה (padah), which means "to redeem" or "to deliver," and יָהּ (Yah), the abbreviated divine name. This name expresses trust in the God who saves and delivers His people. In Israel, proper names often carried significant theological and personal meaning.
H6305K.emploi: Pedaja appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. This unique mention places him at the time of the solemn public reading of the Law by Ezra, after the return from Exile to Jerusalem. The twelve men surrounding him on the platform—including Matthithja, Shema, Anaya, and others—likely formed a group of leaders or priests assisting in the restoration of the religious and civil life of the people. Nothing more is known about his life or specific role in the community.

sens: man of the lineage of Benjamin living during the time of the Exile and the Return
H6305L.detail: Pedaja is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:7, where he appears in a genealogy listing the sons of Benjamin who returned from exile in Babylon. He is the son of Kolaja and the father of Joed.
H6305L.origine: The name Pedaja means "the Lord has redeemed" (from the Hebrew "padah," redeemed, and "Yah," the divine name). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, proclaiming God's saving action. Another character with the same name appears in royal genealogies as the father of Zerubbabel.
H6305L.emploi: Pedaja is cited only once in Nehemiah 11:7, in the context of the lists of those who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile to Babylon. He belongs to the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin and is part of the movement of return and restoration of Israel. Although little known, he represents one of the many ordinary Israelites who participated in the rebuilding of the Jewish community.

sens: Levite in charge of overseeing the temple storerooms under Nehemiah
H6305M.detail: 1. Pedaja is a Levite (a member of the tribe of Levi, reserved for temple service) whom Governor Nehemiah designates to supervise the temple's reserves and storerooms. His name means "the Lord has redeemed." He works alongside the priest Shelemiah and the scribe Zadok, forming a control team responsible for distributing portions fairly to other Levites and priests (Nehemiah 13:13). This office shows the importance placed on honesty and faithfulness in the management of goods dedicated to worship.
H6305M.origine: The name Pedaja comes from two Hebrew elements: "pedya" (ransom, redemption) and "ya" (abbreviation of Yahweh, the Lord). It belongs to a family of theophoric names (containing the name of God) that expressed divine intervention. This type of name was common among Israelites to proclaim trust in divine protection.
H6305M.emploi: Pedaja appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 13:13. He is mentioned as a reliable Levite, chosen by Nehemiah after his return to Jerusalem to inspect the temple storerooms. This passage occurs in the context of Nehemiah's reform, which aimed to restore moral and administrative order in the temple after the exile. The mention of his renowned faithfulness emphasizes that his appointment was based on his reputation for integrity.
H6305M.portee: Pedaja illustrates the role of the Levites upon the return from exile: not only to serve in worship but also to ensure the just management of the community's goods. His story reminds us that integrity in administrative responsibilities is a testimony of faithfulness to God, and that management talents in service to the Church remain an important vocation.

sens: price paid to free someone from servitude or danger
action of recovering something by paying
H6306A.detail: 1. Redemption is primarily the price paid to free a person: money is paid to release someone from a situation where they belong to someone else or where they are held. In Numbers 3:49, Moses collects the money for the "redemption" of the firstborn of Israel who cannot be replaced by the Levites: each child not covered by the Levitical exchange must be "redeemed" by a cash payment to God. 2. By extension, the word also refers to the action itself: not only the price but the entire operation that restores freedom or recovers what was lost. It is to accomplish deliverance through payment.
H6306A.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root פדה (padah), which literally means "to pull out" or "to draw out." The initial image is physical: pulling someone out of a trap or prison. The word pidyon (רִדְיוֹן), of which pidyom is a variant, is formed by adding suffixes to the root padah. This family of words always evokes the idea of liberation obtained through an act or a price: to release, to save, to redeem.
H6306A.emploi: The word pidyom appears only once in Numbers 3:49. It is used in the context of the Levitical system: the Levites are consecrated to God to serve the tabernacle, and this service ritually "replaces" all the male firstborn of Israel (who would otherwise belong to God). However, there are more firstborns than Levites. For the surplus children, Moses must collect a "redemption," that is, a sum of money that pays to release these children from the temple obligation. The redemption here is therefore a substitute price: instead of the child being offered to the temple, the monetary equivalent is paid.
H6306A.portee: This word reminds us that liberation is never free in the biblical economy: it requires a price. It introduces the central idea of Christian redemption: Jesus pays His own blood as the ultimate "price" to redeem humanity from sin and death. Understanding how redemption functions in the Old Testament helps the reader grasp the depth of Christ's sacrifice.

sens: price paid to free someone or something from slavery or danger
liberation obtained by the payment of a compensation
action of regaining possession of what one had lost or ceded
H6306B.detail: 1. Redemption is primarily a price, a sum of money paid to obtain the freedom of a person or to save them. In Exodus 21:30, if an ox kills a man or woman, the owner of the animal can save his own life by paying a redemption — this is the price of his liberation. 2. By extension, redemption refers to the act of liberation itself, the deliverance obtained by payment. In Psalms 49:9, the text states that "the redemption of their soul is costly": this means that an enormous compensation would be required to save the life of the rich man, and that no wealth can truly buy this deliverance. 3. The word can also describe the action of regaining possession — for example, recovering a property pledged by paying the price.
H6306B.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root פדה (padah), which means "to free, to redeem" or "to deliver." It evokes the image of unbinding chains, paying to bring someone out of servitude. The same verb appears in the Pentateuch and the Psalms to speak of the deliverance that Israel experienced in Egypt: God "redeemed" His people, freeing them from slavery by paying a price, in a sense — His divine intervention and strength.
H6306B.emploi: The word פִּדְיוֹן appears twice in biblical Hebrew. In Exodus 21:30, it refers to a financial compensation imposed to save a life: the owner of a dangerous ox can pay a redemption instead of being sentenced to death. In Psalms 49:9, the psalmist asserts that the redemption of the soul — that is, the ransom that could save a human life — is unaffordable and cannot truly be bought, even by riches. The context shows that the idea of redeeming one's life with money is an illusion: only God can truly deliver man from death.
H6306B.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that life has a price — that it is not taken for granted. It also prepares the biblical concept of spiritual redemption: just as a price is paid to free a prisoner or a slave, Christ paid with His life the redemption of our souls. It is a powerful image for understanding the cross: love given as a ransom.

sens: Region of Northern Mesopotamia, between the Euphrates and the Tigris, in Aram (Syria)
Land of origin of Abraham's family, notably the Arameans Bethuel and Laban
H6307.detail:
1. Paddan-Aram is a plain or high plateau located in northern Mesopotamia, in the region called Aram (corresponding to modern-day Syria). The name literally means "the field of Aram." It is a fertile and inhabited region, from which the maternal ancestors of Jacob and the Aramean families of the Bible originate. 

2. In the Genesis narrative, it is first the place from which Rebecca, Isaac's wife, comes: she is "the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean, of Paddan-Aram" (Genesis 25:20). Then, it is the land where Jacob exiles himself to escape Esau's anger and to find a wife: Isaac blesses him and sends him there, saying "Go to Paddan-Aram" (Genesis 28:2). Jacob stays there for a long time, accumulating wives, children, and flocks, before returning to Canaan with his family (Genesis 31:18).
H6307.origine: The Hebrew word פַּדָּן (paddan) literally means "field" or "plain." Paddan-Aram thus means "the field of Aram" or "the plain of Aram." This toponym designates a well-identified historical region of ancient Mesopotamia, that of the Arameans, to which the patriarchs are closely linked by their family origins.
H6307.emploi: Paddan-Aram appears 11 times in Genesis, exclusively in the patriarchal narrative. It is mentioned mainly in chapter 28, when Isaac sends Jacob there to find a wife (Genesis 28:2, 28:5, 28:6, 28:7). It is also where Jacob's sons are born (Genesis 35:26) and where Israel learns that his wife Rachel has died there (Genesis 48:7). The narrative emphasizes that it is a land of Aram, a "foreign" land compared to Canaan, from which Abraham's family takes their wives to preserve their lineage and faith.
H6307.portee: Paddan-Aram reminds us that the patriarchs did not always live in Canaan: they come from a distant region, themselves migrants. This land is the cradle of the chosen family, but also the place of exile and trial for Jacob. It shows how God guided His own even in a foreign land and how He protected the promise by preserving the purity of the lineage through suitable alliances.

sens: Save someone from danger or death
Free from the pit, that is, from destruction
H6308.detail:
1. To save someone from danger or death: the verb means to pull away from immediate peril. In Job 33:24, the angel intervenes to deliver the man from descending into the pit, that is, from death and the realm of the dead.
2. To free from the pit: this meaning is more precise — it refers to saving someone who is about to fall or descend into destruction. The context of Job shows how divine compassion intervenes to spare death from one who is at risk of perishing.
H6308.origine: The Hebrew word פָּדַע comes from a root that evokes the idea of extracting or pulling away. It is close to roots meaning "ransom" or "price of redemption" (פָּדָה, padah), which suggests the image of a liberation at a price or exchange. The verb is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible, and its exact usage remains somewhat obscure.
H6308.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved Hebrew biblical text: in Job 33:24. It designates the action of the angel or divine messenger who intervenes on behalf of the dying person to save him from the pit — that is, from death and perdition. It is a decisive moment where divine mercy, through a heavenly intercessor, snatches man from the misfortune that threatens him.
H6308.portee: This rare word shows that God does not abandon man to death. Even at the threshold of destruction, God's compassionate intervention can still save him, provided that a "ransom" is found — an image of grace that pays the price of our liberation. It is a word of hope for those who believe they are lost.

sens: Fatty part of an animal's body, notably the peritoneal fat around internal organs
Fat substance burned as an offering on the altar of sacrifice
H6309.detail:
1. Fat refers to the fatty part of the body of the sacrificed animal, particularly the fat that envelops the intestines and internal organs. It is a rich, precious, and nourishing substance, representing the best of the animal. In Leviticus 1:8 and 1:12, it must be placed on the wood of the altar with the pieces and the head of the offered animal.
2. Fat holds a fundamental religious significance: it is the part intended to be entirely burned as an offering. Unlike the meat, which was often eaten, the fat was reserved for God alone, showing that it is the best that the faithful offer to Him. In Leviticus 8:20, Moses completely burns the head, the pieces, and the fat of the ram, fulfilling the ordination rite of the priests.
H6309.origine: The Hebrew word péder comes from a root designating abundance and wealth. It applies to the fat that covers and protects vital organs, considered in the ancient Near East as the most precious and energetic part of the animal. That is why it was reserved for offerings to God, never for common consumption.
H6309.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in Leviticus, at the heart of the prescriptions on sacrifices. In Leviticus 1:8 and 1:12, it refers to the burnt offering or sin offering of birds or large cattle. In Leviticus 8:20, the fat is part of the installation rite of the priests. Each time, it must be completely burned on the altar — never eaten, never shared with the people. It is a constant practice of worship: to offer to God the best part, that which is reserved for Him.
H6309.portee: The sacrificed fat teaches the believer that serving God does not consist of giving Him one's leftovers or what costs little, but offering Him what is most precious. It reminds us that certain things belong to God alone, not for human profit. It is an invitation to true generosity and respect for what is consecrated.

sens: Opening of the face through which one eats and speaks
What comes out of the mouth: the word, the words
What comes from the word: what has been promised or commanded
Opening or entrance of a thing (well, river, cave)
Mouth or jaw of an animal
Extremity, edge, mouth
H6310G.detail:
1. The mouth is the opening of the face, the organ of speech and nourishment. This is the most direct and common sense. Moses asks God: "Who has given a mouth to man?" (Exodus 4:11), referring to what allows one to eat and speak.
2. The mouth often refers to what comes out of it: words, the spoken word. "The mouth of the fool brings ruin upon him" (Proverbs 18:7): it is through his words that he destroys himself. "Truth has disappeared... from their mouth" (Jeremiah 7:28) means that they no longer speak the truth.
3. The mouth can also refer to the commitment or order that emanates from it: what has been said becomes a binding word. Jephthah says to his daughter: "Do to me according to what has come out of your mouth" (Judges 11:36) — he must honor his word.
4. The mouth is the opening of a thing. In Genesis 29:2-3, the mouth of the well is its surface, through which one accesses it. It is also the mouth of a watercourse.
5. The mouth or jaw of an animal, such as that of a lion or a serpent, which is referred to by its mouth (1 Samuel 17:35).
6. The extremity or edge of a region, the mouth of a river.
H6310G.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּה (peh) has its root in the idea of opening, of slit. It is close to פִּיָּה (piyyah), which also means "mouth" or "opening." This root simply evokes the orifice: it is through the mouth that one speaks and eats. The Hebrews naturally designated by the same word any main opening of a thing — that of a well, a cave, a river — because the mouth is the most important opening of the body.
H6310G.emploi: The word peh (mouth) is one of the most frequent words in the Old Testament: 308 occurrences. It appears in all books and contexts. Its use extends: in the primary sense, the physical mouth (Exodus 4:11: "Who has given a mouth to man?"); in the sense of word, what comes out of the mouth (Proverbs 18:7: "The mouth of the fool brings ruin upon him"); to the idea of commitment or order (Judges 11:36: honoring one's word); to natural openings (Genesis 29:2-3: the mouth of the well); to animals (1 Samuel 17:35: the mouth of the lion); to geographical extremities (the mouth of a river). The context alone determines the exact meaning, but the central image remains that of the opening and what comes out of it.
H6310G.portee: The "mouth" reminds the believer of the power of the word. In biblical Hebrew, the word is not just wind: what comes out of the mouth of God or a man creates, binds, and transforms. Our words bless or curse us (Proverbs 18:7). This frequency of the word invites us to watch what comes out of our mouth, to measure the weight of our promises and our words.

sens: Sharp edge of a cutting weapon, particularly a sword
Extremity or edge of a thing (well, river, territory)
Opening, orifice through which one speaks or breathes
Mouth of an animal
Word or command that comes from the mouth
H6310H.detail:
1. The edge is the sharp and cutting side of a sword or a cutting weapon: it is the side that wounds and kills. The expression "by the edge of the sword" frequently appears in battle narratives to describe slaughter in combat (Exodus 17:13, Joshua 10:28, Judges 4:15).
2. It is also the extremity or edge of something: the end of a territory from one end to the other (Ezra 9:11), the opening of a well or a river through which water flows.
3. In a more concrete sense, it refers to the human mouth, the opening through which one speaks and breathes, and from which words come out.
4. It also applies to the mouths of animals, such as horses or wild beasts.
5. By extension, the word can designate the word itself or a command: what comes from the mouth of God or a leader is powerful and binding.
H6310H.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּה (peh) literally means "mouth," the visible opening of the face. From this concrete image comes the sense of "edge" or "extremity": one speaks of the "peh" (edge) of a sword as one speaks of the "opening" of a weapon, which cuts. The word thus enriches to designate anything that is a limit, a boundary, a sharp ridge. The notion of word also naturally derives from the mouth as the source of speech.
H6310H.emploi: The word appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings). Its most frequent sense (27 times) is "edge of the sword" in contexts of battle and conquest: Joshua destroys cities "by the edge of the sword" (Joshua 10:28, 11:11), Barak defeats Sisera in this manner (Judges 4:15). The term also appears to designate an edge or extremity: "from one end to the other" of the land (Ezra 9:11). In the poetic books (Psalms, Proverbs, Job), it can evoke the word, the mouth, or even the blade (the edge) of a weapon. Its usage is concrete and realistic: it describes the brutal reality of war and the destructive power of the sword.
H6310H.portee: This word reminds the believer that the sword, an instrument of destruction, was the tool of divine will during the conquest of Canaan. But it also reveals how the word comes from the mouth: everything that comes from the mouth has power, either to destroy or to build up. The believer is invited to reflect on the weight of his own words and to recognize that only the word of God endures.

sens: Command, instruction given by an authority
Word, spoken word that establishes what must be done
Directive, instruction to follow in an action or work
Judicial statement or testimony given before a court
H6310I.detail:
1. The word designates the command of an authority — one who has the power to speak and decide imposes his will. Pharaoh says to Joseph: "All my people will obey your orders" (Genesis 41:40), and God commands that the Levites be counted "at the order of the Lord by Moses" (Numbers 4:49). It is the mouth that commands, and others must obey.
2. The word is also used for the word spoken once, the particular statement: Joshua "will go out at the order of Eleazar" (Numbers 27:21), meaning according to what he has declared. The word that comes from the mouth fixes the action.
3. It can also designate the written or transmitted instruction for a specific task: Jeremiah dictates his message to the scribe Baruch "according to the dictation" of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 36:4), word for word what must be reproduced.
4. Before the court, it is the deposition, the word given in testimony: the Law requires "two or three witnesses" and their word establishes the fact (Deuteronomy 17:6).
H6310I.origine: The Hebrew word peh literally means "mouth," the organ through which one speaks. From there comes the sense of "order" or "word": it is the word that comes from the mouth, especially that of an authority. The word is very ancient and is found in all Semitic languages. The family also includes words meaning "two-edged" (the sword with two mouths, two blades) and "surface" (the mouth of the well, the visible opening).
H6310I.emploi: The word appears 76 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is particularly frequent in the books of Moses and Joshua, where it designates the orders that God or His representatives give to the people: orders for marching, counting, distributing work. In the prophets (especially Jeremiah), it takes on the meaning of transcribed prophetic word. In Moses, it signifies what God says to the people, what must be obeyed. The three main translations are "order" (46 times, the dominant sense), "mouth" (8 times, the original sense that remains), "dictation" (5 times, when it involves faithfully rendering a word). The context always shows that it is the word of an authority that creates the obligation.
H6310I.portee: This word teaches that the word of an authority — especially that of God — is not a mere suggestion: it creates an obligation. It must be listened to and obeyed. For the believer, this reminds us that the Word of God is never neutral; it establishes what must be. This is also why a lightly spoken word is dangerous: it comes from the mouth and engages the one who has spoken it.

sens: Mouth of a person or an animal
Opening, orifice of an object or structure
Entry or passage of a container, well, or river
H6310J.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the mouth — the organ through which one speaks, breathes, and eats. This is the primary and most natural meaning, even if the provided usages do not show this direct application.
2. It extends to any comparable opening: the opening made in the middle of a priest's robe (Exodus 28:32), through which the head passes, or the crown of a bronze base, which forms a round opening (1 Kings 7:31).
3. More broadly, it refers to the entry or passage of a hollow object or structure — the opening of an ephah (large container) on which a lead cover is placed (Zechariah 5:8). The common image is that of a "door" through which one accesses something.
H6310J.origine: The Hebrew word peh literally means "mouth" or "opening." It comes from a primitive root whose basic image is that of an orifice, a passage. The mouth is concretely the main opening of the human and animal body, and the word naturally extends to any analogous physical opening: doors, orifices, passages. It is a very common word in biblical Hebrew.
H6310J.emploi: The word appears dozens of times in the Old Testament, but the Segond 1910 primarily translates it as "opening" in technical passages where it describes material objects: the garments of worship (Exodus 28:32 and 39:23), the furniture of the temple (1 Kings 7:31), the containers (Zechariah 5:8). A figurative usage appears in Job 36:16 ("to set you at large"), where the word evokes the idea of breadth and freedom — the metaphorical opening that deliverance offers. Thus, the word encompasses both the material and concrete opening as well as the spiritual image of liberation.
H6310J.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the mouth and speech are concrete realities: our words come from a physical opening and engage our responsibility before God. The image of the opening also invites us to meditate on what opens us — the grace that liberates and enlarges us, as in Job 36:16. It is a humble, incarnate word that brings faith back to the body and visible things.

sens: Opening, entry of a cavity or passage
Quantity fixed according to a measure or rule
Part, portion assigned to someone
Agreement, common consent
H6310K.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the opening or entry — literally the mouth of a person or an animal, but also the mouth of a well or a river. It is the image of a passage or a marked limit.
2. By extension, "peh" means a determined quantity according to a precise rule: "according to the number" (Genesis 47:12), "what was needed" of manna each morning (Exodus 16:21), or what each should take "according to" their needs or portion.
3. The word is used to designate the portion or inheritance assigned: "a double portion" to the firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:17), or the shares distributed to the tribes (Numbers 26:54).
4. It can finally express agreement or consensus: "of one accord" (2 Chronicles 18:12), meaning "with one mouth," all speaking with one voice.
H6310K.origine: The Hebrew word "peh" first means "mouth" and comes from a root evoking opening. From there, the idea of "word" (what comes out of the mouth) and, by logical extension, that of "proportion" or "ratio" arises — what is measured, what comes from a fixed rule as words come from the mouth. This is a typical example where the concrete image of the body produces abstract and measured meanings.
H6310K.emploi: The word "peh" appears 31 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in laws and historical narratives. It is rarely used alone to refer to the mouth — other phrases are used — but most often in expressions of proportion or measure: "according to the mouth of" means "in measure of." The usages show this evolution: first the idea of "what is needed" or "what is suitable" (Exodus 16:21, Leviticus 27:8), then that of "assigned part" according to law or inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17, Numbers 26:54), and finally the agreement of several "with one mouth" (2 Chronicles 18:12). The context is very often that of sharing, inheritance, or law.
H6310K.portee: This word reminds the believer that every sharing, every inheritance, every portion of life comes according to a fixed and just measure. God distributes not at random, but "according to" — according to justice, according to needs, according to promise. It is an invitation to accept one's portion from God's hand as being just and sufficient, even if it seems unequal in human eyes.

sens: One of the three equal parts of a whole
The price of a tool repair
The part of a population destined to survive
H6310L.detail: 1. A third is one of the three equal parts into which something is divided: if you divide a cake into three identical pieces, each is a third of the cake. In 1 Samuel 13:21, the word refers to a unit of weight (a third of a shekel) paid for sharpening tools, such as the plows and hoes of the Israelite farmers. 2. It is therefore also the price or fraction of a monetary value. 3. Figuratively, when speaking of population, a third means the portion of a group that survives after a trial: in Zechariah 13:8, a third of the people will remain alive while two-thirds perish during the judgment of the Lord.
H6310L.origine: The Hebrew word peh literally means "mouth" or "opening." The meaning of "third" or "one-third" derives from it: one measures by weight, and a third of a shekel was a standard weight unit in Israel. The word belongs to the family of numbers and divisions, used to express proportions and shares.
H6310L.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with the meaning of "third." In 1 Samuel 13:21, it designates a fraction of a shekel, the monetary weight unit used to pay for sharpening agricultural tools — a concrete and everyday economic context. In Zechariah 13:8, it expresses a proportion in a prophetic vision: the three thirds of the people are divided, two-thirds are struck down, and one-third survives. This last usage gives the number a theological significance, associated with judgment and the divine grace that preserves a remnant.
H6310L.portee: This word reminds us that God counts and measures precisely what He does. In Zechariah, the image of the third that survives speaks of God's faithfulness: even in judgment, He preserves a remnant of His people. For the believer, it is an assurance that God never completely destroys, but always reserves a posterity for those who belong to Him.

sens: The place where one is, at this moment or at this point in the narrative
On the side of, nearby, close to
From here (indication of distance or duration from the present)
H6311.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: the place where the action takes place, where one is now. When Lot must flee Sodom, he is told: "Who do you still have here? Sons-in-law, sons and daughters, and all that belongs to you in the city, bring them out of this place" (Genesis 19:12). The word indicates the place of immediate danger.
2. By extension, "here" designates a side, a spatial position, especially in passages that describe architecture or an object. In Ezekiel's vision of the temple, it speaks of "two tables on each side": it is the word "here" that marks this lateral proximity (Ezekiel 40:39).
3. When one adds "from here to three days" or "from here", the word takes on a temporal nuance: it means "from now, from the present". The king says to Amasa: "Summon me the men of Judah from here to three days" (2 Samuel 20:4), indicating a deadline that begins at that moment.
H6311.origine: The Hebrew פֹּה (poh) is a very ancient adverb of place, likely formed from a root that expresses proximity or immediate presence. The word belongs to the family of simple and direct Hebrew adverbs. It is found throughout the Old Testament, often associated with gestures or calls: "Follow me from here!" or "Stay here". Its equivalent in English, "here", captures this same warmth of presence and immediacy.
H6311.emploi: The word appears 57 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It primarily serves to designate the present place in a dialogue or action: one tells someone to stay "here", to leave "from here", or one asks "who is here?". The Psalms and the prophets (especially Ezekiel) use it to fix a precise spatial position, particularly in descriptions of the temple. In passages from Deuteronomy, "here" emphasizes physical presence: "it is with those who are here among us, present this day before the Lord our God" (29:15), highlighting that the covenant concerns the people gathered at that moment.
H6311.portee: This small word reminds us that God speaks to the people and to each believer in the concrete, the present, the place where they are. "Here" is the place of encounter with God, the moment when His word addresses us now. It teaches us to seek God's will not in the abstract, but in the reality of our present life.

sens: son of Issachar
ancestor of a family of the people of Israel
H6312G.detail:
1. Puva is a man belonging to the tribe of Issachar, mentioned for the first time during the descent into Egypt at the time of Moses. He is one of the sons of Issachar, along with his brothers Tola, Job, and Shimron. His name also appears in the variants "Pua" and "Phuvah".
2. Puva is best known as the ancestor of a family called the Puvites, which bears his name and is among the families of the tribe of Issachar during the census of the people in the wilderness.
H6312G.origine: The name Puva means "splendid" or "bright" in Hebrew. It designates an ancestor who gave his name to his descendants, according to the custom of Israel: his descendants were called Puvites and formed one of the important families of the tribe of Issachar.
H6312G.emploi: Puva is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 46:13, he is listed among the sons of Issachar who went down to Egypt with Jacob. In Numbers 26:23, during the second census of the people in the wilderness, he is named as the ancestor of the family of the Puvites. In 1 Chronicles 7:1, the genealogy of Issachar mentions him again. These three passages place him in the time of Egypt and the wilderness, as the founder of one of the great families of Issachar.

sens: Man of Israel, father of Tola the judge
H6312H.detail: Pua is a character in the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Tola, who became a judge of Israel after Abimelech and rose up to deliver the people (Judges 10:1). Pua himself belonged to the tribe of Issachar and lived during the time of the judges, before the monarchy was established in Israel.
H6312H.origine: The name Pua means "splendid" or "bright". It was borne by several individuals in the ancient generations of Israel: a son of Issachar (mentioned in the genealogy of the tribes), and this Pua mentioned in the book of Judges, a man of Issachar and father of the judge Tola. The name also appears in forms such as "Pue" or "Phuvah" according to different genealogical lists.
H6312H.emploi: Pua is cited only once in the Holy Scriptures, in Judges 10:1, where he is presented as the father of Tola. It is through this family link that we know him: he is the ancestor of the judge who governed Israel and delivered it after the troubles caused by Abimelech. Although not well known, Pua belongs to the lineage of men whom God used to guide His people during the time of the judges.

sens: To lose all strength, to become weak and inert
To be paralyzed by emotion or shock
To cease to make an effort, to give up
To be insensitive or indifferent
H6313.detail:
1. The word first describes the physical state of one who loses their vigor: their body no longer responds, their limbs feel numb. Jacob is the most striking image of this: when he learns that Joseph is still alive, "the heart of Jacob remained cold" (Genesis 45:26) — it is the shock that freezes him, rendering him incapable of reacting normally.
2. It is also the experience of one whose strength is exhausted: the psalmist cries, "I am without strength, completely broken" (Psalms 38:9), describing a complete weakening of body and soul under the weight of suffering.
3. The verb can also mean to cease making an effort, to let oneself go. When the psalmist says, "my hands are stretched out without tiring" (Psalms 77:3), he expresses a prayer that does not stop — the opposite of numbness would be to give up.
4. By extension, it means to become indifferent or insensitive to what should touch or motivate us — a form of spiritual or moral apathy.
H6313.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of stiffening, becoming inactive or frozen. The primary root suggests the image of the body becoming numb, as when one is cold or paralyzed by shock. The word belongs to a family of expressions that describe the loss of vitality and movement.
H6313.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Old Testament, mainly in contexts of emotional or spiritual crisis. In Genesis 45:26, it accounts for Jacob's astonishment at an incredible news — his heart "freezes", he cannot believe. In the Psalms (38:9 and 77:3), it expresses the exhaustion of the faithful who suffers and whose strength is draining away. In Habakkuk 1:4, the context suggests inaction or paralysis in the face of evil. The word thus oscillates between paralyzing emotion, physical and spiritual fatigue, and inaction.
H6313.portee: This word reminds the reader that spiritual fatigue is real and can paralyze us. It is an image for those who go through suffering and feel their strength leaving them: the Bible acknowledges this reality without denying it. It also invites us to recognize when we become numb in the face of God's will — when shock, doubt, or weariness freeze us. It is a call to regain our spiritual vigor and to persevere in prayer despite exhaustion.

sens: Interruption, pause, temporary stop of an activity
Rest, relaxation after effort
Relief, respite from suffering or sorrow
H6314.detail:
1. This word denotes the interruption or suspension of an activity: a moment when one stops doing something. In Lamentations 2:18, it refers to the release of the cry, of lamentation: the prophet commands the wall of Zion not to cease its weeping, to cry "without release," meaning without interruption.
2. By extension, it is the rest or relaxation that follows an effort: a pause where the body and mind regain strength. It is the opposite of tension and continuous labor.
3. It is also the relief or respite, particularly in the face of suffering. In the context of lamentation and pain, asking for a release would be seeking a moment of consolation or alleviation of sorrow.
H6314.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of stopping or cessation. The family of related words revolves around the notion of suspension or pause: ceasing an effort, not continuing. It is a simple and concrete term, borrowed from the experience of physical rest.
H6314.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Lamentations 2:18. It is used in a command addressed to the wall of Zion (personified as a suffering creature): the wall must weep without release, without interruption, day and night. The expression "give yourself no release" means: do not cease to cry, do not rest in your lamentation. It is a call for the continuity of the expression of grief and sorrow in the face of the destruction of Jerusalem.
H6314.portee: This word reminds us that in moments of deep pain and intercession, there is a place for perseverance and the absence of spiritual cowardice. It invites the believer not to turn away too quickly from their own pain or that of others, but to bear it faithfully before God, without release.

sens: Breathe, produce wind with the mouth or nose
Emit a sound of breath or disdain
Incite to quarrel, anger, or discord
Pronounce, say with force or conviction
Refresh with a breeze
Produce a loud noise or violent movement
H6315.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of vital breath: to breathe, or to intentionally produce a flow of air through the mouth or nose — as one blows on a fire to stoke it (Proverbs 29:8: "The mockers blow fire in the city").
2. By extension, "blow" evokes a sound of disdain, contempt, or challenge — when someone "blows against" their adversaries, they show their rage or contempt towards them (Psalms 10:5).
3. An important figurative sense: to incite, excite someone to quarrel or unfair action. A false witness who "says" (literally "blows") lies (Proverbs 6:19) somewhat launches accusations; he "blows" discord between brothers.
4. By metaphor of breath that conveys a word, "blow" means to pronounce or say with force — the false witness "blows" a lie, he states it with assurance (Proverbs 14:5).
5. In a gentle physical sense, a breeze can "refresh" — before the day "refreshes," meaning before the heat declines with the evening wind (Song of Solomon 4:6).
6. The word can also evoke a violent breath, a noise or tumultuous event — God can "blow" His fury (Ezekiel 21:36).
H6315.origine: The verb puach comes from a Hebrew root expressing the movement of wind and air. The basic image is that of vital breath or wind blowing — hence all the derived meanings: sound, expulsion of air, force, agitation. This verb appears mainly in biblical poetry and in proverbs, where it illustrates behaviors or forces that "escape" from man (lies, anger, contempt, words).
H6315.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs and the Song of Solomon. In Proverbs, "blowing" lies is an image for saying them with assurance and malice: the false witness "blows" (Proverbs 6:19, 14:5, 19:5). When the mockers "blow fire," they stir up anger and quarrel in the city (Proverbs 29:8). In the Song, the wind "blows" or "refreshes": it is the evening breeze that calms the heat (Song of Solomon 4:6, 4:16). In poetry, the verb also expresses rage or contempt (Psalms 10:5) and divine fury (Ezekiel 21:36). The meaning evolves from the physical (the wind blows) to the moral (uttering words, inciting discord).
H6315.portee: This word reminds us that speech is a force — it "blows" from us like the wind. Proverbs invites us to see in the lies of the false witness not a simple error, but an action that "blows" discord and destruction. Conversely, the breeze that "refreshes" in the Song evokes peace and tenderness. The Bible invites us to be careful about what we "blow" — our lies, our anger, our accusations — for these words act as a force in the world.

sens: son of Ham, mentioned in the genealogies of antiquity
people or region of ancient North Africa, probably Libya
H6316G.detail:
1. Put is a son of Ham listed in the primitive genealogy of Genesis (Genesis 10:6); he also appears in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:8. He is listed alongside his brothers Cush, Mizraim, and Canaan, as an ancestor of a branch of humanity after the flood.
2. Put also designates a people or region of North Africa, probably identified with ancient Libya or a coastal territory of that region. This name likely reflects a historical or genealogical link between the peoples of the Mediterranean basin and those of North Africa in the memory of the ancient Hebrews.
H6316G.origine: The name Put literally means "a bow" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a characteristic weapon or a martial quality. This root emphasizes the image of a martial people or a territory known for its archers. The name mainly appears in the genealogies of Genesis 10 and 1 Chronicles 1, which list the peoples dispersed after the flood according to the biblical view of the ancient world.
H6316G.emploi: Put is mentioned only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:6 and in 1 Chronicles 1:8. In these two passages, he occupies the same rank among the four sons of Ham, indicating his importance in the geography and ethnography of the known world of the ancient Israelites. The genealogical context suggests that the biblical writers considered Put as a founding ancestor of a distinct people, probably located in North Africa. The absence of other specific biblical accounts concerning Put suggests that this people did not play a central role in the history of Israel, unlike Egypt or Canaan.

sens: people and nation from North Africa, probably from Libya
warriors carrying shields and helmets, allies of great powers
H6316H.detail: Puth designates a people and a nation located in North Africa, most likely the Libyans or a related group. The Bible always mentions it alongside Ethiopia and other nations in a military context: they are warriors recognized for their equipment (shields, helmets, bows) and their status as auxiliaries or powerful allies. In Jeremiah 46:9, they fight alongside Ethiopia, bearing shields. In Ezekiel 27:10, they serve in the army of Tyre as men of war. In Nahum 3:9, they support Nineveh as auxiliaries. Thus, Puth represents a respected military force of the ancient world, capable of mobilizing well-equipped troops.
H6316H.origine: The name Puth (פּוּט in Hebrew) literally means "a bow" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the bow as the characteristic weapon of these warriors. The Bible regularly associates it with Lud, Cush (Ethiopia), and the Libyans, suggesting that this people held an important place in the geopolitics of the ancient Middle East and Africa. A variant of the name, "Pul" (פּוּל), is also attested in biblical texts.
H6316H.emploi: Puth appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Nahum). In each occurrence, it is mentioned in contexts of great military coalitions or warrior powers. In Jeremiah 46:9, during the battle against Egypt, Puth fights with Ethiopia. In Ezekiel 27:10, it is a force in the army of Tyre. In Ezekiel 30:5 and 38:5, it is among the nations that fall or rise in alliance. Finally, in Nahum 3:9, it is the auxiliary of besieged Nineveh. These usages confirm that Puth is always presented as an influential warrior people, associated with the great powers of its time.

sens: man whose daughter married Eleazar, son of Aaron
H6317.detail: Puthiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Moses and Aaron establish the genealogies of the Levites. He is known only as the father of Eleazar's wife, the son of Aaron. This woman gave birth to Phinehas, who would become a high priest and whose descendants would play an important role in the history of Israel (Exodus 6:25).
H6317.origine: The name Puthiel means "afflicted by God" or "God afflicts." It is a Hebrew name composed of two elements: a root evoking affliction or suffering, and the divine name El (God). Although no details are given about his life, his name may suggest a condition of suffering or trial that this man experienced.
H6317.emploi: Puthiel appears only once in the entire Bible, in Exodus 6:25. He is simply identified as the father of Eleazar's wife, one of the priests from Aaron's lineage. This genealogical passage aims to establish the descendants of the Levites and show how the priesthood was perpetuated. The only interest in mentioning Puthiel is to trace the lineage that led to Phinehas, a much better-known figure who would receive the covenant of the eternal priesthood.

sens: Egyptian officer in the service of Pharaoh
Chief of the guards or executioner of Pharaoh
Master who bought Joseph as a slave
H6318.detail:
1. Potiphar is an important Egyptian figure from the time of the Patriarchs, holding a trusted official position with Pharaoh. He is the one who buys Joseph when the Ishmaelites sell him in Egypt (Genesis 39:1).
2. His title of "chief of the guards" or "chief of the executioners" shows that he occupies a position of military or judicial responsibility in the Egyptian hierarchy: he is not a mere official, but a man of power.
3. He becomes Joseph's master as a purchased slave, a relationship that constitutes the starting point of Joseph's long stay in Egypt and his subsequent rise to a position of authority in the country.
H6318.origine: The name Potiphar literally means "belonging to the sun" in ancient Egyptian. It is a compound name that reflects the religious culture of Egypt, where the sun (Ra) was a major deity. The name evokes the cultural and religious environment of pharaonic Egypt.
H6318.emploi: Potiphar appears twice in Genesis, in chapters 37 and 39, at the time when Joseph is sold in Egypt. In Genesis 37:36, the Midianites sell Joseph to Potiphar, "officer of Pharaoh, chief of the guards." In Genesis 39:1, the narrative resumes: Potiphar, the same Egyptian figure, buys Joseph from the Ishmaelites. These two closely related mentions mark the decisive turning point in Joseph's life — his sale into slavery and his entry into the service of a powerful Egyptian master, where he will experience trials and ultimately remarkable favor.
H6318.portee: The figure of Potiphar illustrates how God directs the events of a believer's life even in adversity and oppression. Although Joseph is reduced to slavery, God accompanies Joseph to Potiphar and gives him wisdom that earns his master's trust. This is an example of divine Providence in difficult circumstances.

sens: Egyptian priest of On, father of Asenath
figure from the patriarchal times
H6319.detail: Poti-Phéra is an Egyptian priest attached to the temple of the sun god Ra in the city of On. He is the one to whom Pharaoh gives his daughter, Asenath, in marriage to honor Joseph and integrate him into Egyptian high society (Genesis 41:45). Through this marital alliance, Poti-Phéra becomes Joseph's father-in-law and the grandfather of the two sons Joseph will have in Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50; 46:20).
H6319.origine: The Egyptian name Poti-Phéra literally means "he whom Ra has given." It combines the Egyptian title *poti* ("he of") and the name of the great Egyptian sun god Ra. It is a typically Egyptian name that reflects the piety of Egyptian priests towards their deities.
H6319.emploi: Poti-Phéra appears only three times in the Bible, always in the account of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 41 and 46). He is always presented as "priest of On" — which underscores his prestigious religious status in Egypt. His role in the biblical text is limited but significant: he facilitates Joseph's integration into Egyptian society by giving him his daughter in marriage, and it is through this union that Asenath becomes the mother of the ancestors of two of the twelve tribes of Israel. Although the Bible recounts nothing more about his life or deeds, his presence in the text marks Joseph's acceptance by the religious and political ruling class of Egypt.
H6319.portee: The mention of Poti-Phéra illustrates how God opened the highest doors of Egypt to Joseph, even giving him an honorable place in the family of a great Egyptian priest. This detail emphasizes that divine favor upon Joseph manifested concretely, even in a pagan land, and ensured his posterity, as his sons, born of this marriage, became the leaders of two major tribes of Israel.

sens: Black cosmetic used to enhance the eyes
Shiny mineral substance intended for adornment or beautification
Substance applied to the eyelids to highlight the gaze
H6320.detail:
1. The cosmetic is a black makeup specifically designed to enhance the eyes and emphasize the gaze. Jezebel applies it before showing herself at the window (2 Kings 9:30), seeking to beautify her appearance. It is a practice of seduction and self-enhancement, characteristic of vanity or pride.
2. The word also refers to a shiny and colored mineral substance used as an ornament or precious stone. In 1 Chronicles 29:2, the cosmetic is among the valuable materials used to decorate the temple of God, alongside gold and sapphires.
3. Generally, it is a substance applied to oneself to adorn and make oneself more attractive. Jeremiah 4:30 speaks of it as a vain attempt at beautification: even adorned with cosmetics, the nation humbles itself and does not achieve what it hopes for.
H6320.origine: The Hebrew word pukh originally refers to antimony or stibium, a black powdered mineral substance that was ground and used to coat the eyelids. This cosmetic was widely used in the ancient Near East. The term extends to anything shiny or colored, used for adornment or beautification.
H6320.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to beautification. Three occurrences designate it as eye makeup: Jezebel uses it before challenging Jehu (2 Kings 9:30), and Jeremiah ironically mentions it, showing that beauty efforts are vain in the face of divine judgment (Jeremiah 4:30). One occurrence places it among the precious stones decorating the temple (1 Chronicles 29:2), where it symbolizes the wealth and splendor of God's house. The biblical context is often critical: the cosmetic becomes a sign of human vanity or misplaced trust in appearance.
H6320.portee: The cosmetic in the Bible is a call to vigilance: it reminds us that external beautification, however alluring, cannot replace inner beauty or obedience to God. Jezebel and the nation described by Jeremiah seek to save themselves through their appearance, in vain. For the Christian, the word invites examination of where their trust lies: in what is seen or in what endures.

sens: Legume cultivated for its edible seeds
Staple food in ancient diets, consumed dried or roasted
H6321.detail: 1. The broad bean is a plant that produces pods containing round and flattened seeds, varying in color depending on the variety. These seeds can be eaten fresh or, more often, harvested and dried for long-term storage. In 2 Samuel 17:28, broad beans are among the provisions brought to David in flight, alongside wheat and barley: it is a robust and nourishing food. 2. In the diet of the biblical world, the broad bean is an essential element, often associated with other grains and legumes. Ezekiel 4:9 shows the prophet commanded to make survival bread mixing broad beans, lentils, millet, and other grains: this mixture illustrates both the poverty of resources during a siege and the recognized nutritional importance of broad beans to sustain the body for a long time.
H6321.origine: The Hebrew word פּוֹל (pol) designates the broad bean by its simple and direct name. It is a well-known plant in the ancient Near East, cultivated for millennia. The same plant is referred to in Greek by related terms, and the broad bean regularly appears in biblical food lists alongside wheat, barley, and lentils, showing its established status as a fundamental legume.
H6321.emploi: The word פּוֹל appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of food supply. In 2 Samuel 17:28, it is one of the foods given to David and his hungry companions during their flight. In Ezekiel 4:9, God commands the prophet to make a mixed bread including broad beans, to symbolize the reduced and mixed sustenance during the siege of Jerusalem. In both cases, the broad bean is never a luxury food, but a practical, durable, and nourishing resource, available in quantity and essential for survival.
H6321.portee: The mention of broad beans invites the reader to recognize the value of simple provisions and ordinary foods that God provides. It reminds us that God's faithfulness often manifests through the basic and concrete resources of daily life, not through the spectacular. For the Christian, it is a lesson in gratitude for daily food and an acknowledgment that God meets the essential needs of His people, even through the humblest means.

sens: King of Assyria in the 8th century BC
Another name for Tiglath-Pileser III
H6322G.detail: 1. Pul is the name by which the Scriptures refer to a king of Assyria who reigns during the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. In 2 Kings 15:19, King Menahem of Israel pays him a thousand talents of silver to obtain his military support and strengthen his threatened throne. He is a powerful sovereign, capable of influencing the political and military affairs of the Levant. 2. Pul is another name, likely his Babylonian nickname, for Tiglath-Pileser III, the great warrior king of Assyria. This dual naming reflects how the same historical figure could be known by different names depending on the regions and traditions. In 1 Chronicles 5:26, he is also called Tilgath-Pilneser, and it is he who deports the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh into captivity, marking one of the significant moments of divine punishment on Israel.
H6322G.origine: The name "Pul" is the Hebrew form of a Babylonian nickname for the great king Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria. This nickname might mean "distinguishing" in English, that is, one who stands out or establishes distinction. Tiglath-Pileser is his full Assyrian name (תִּגְלַת פִּלְאֶסֶר in Hebrew). Extra-biblical historical sources confirm that he is the same historical figure, one of the greatest Assyrian warriors of the 8th century BC.
H6322G.emploi: Pul appears twice in the Hebrew Scriptures, both related to the political history of divided Israel. In 2 Kings 15:19, he intervenes as a mercenary ally of King Menahem, showing that even the kings of Israel sought the support of great powers. In 1 Chronicles 5:26, he executes divine judgment against the northern tribes, taking them into captivity. Both passages designate him as a powerful and feared king of Assyria, whose actions shape the destiny of God's people. His intervention marks a crucial turning point in Israel's history.
H6322G.portee: The mention of Pul reminds the reader that God uses the powers of the world to accomplish His purposes, whether it is a temporary protection granted to a king who pays tribute or judgment against Israel's unfaithfulness. These accounts show that even when Israel seems dominated by foreign empires, it is God who controls history. This strengthens the believer's faith: no earthly power can act outside the sovereign will of the God of Israel.

sens: Name of a region or an African people mentioned alongside distant nations
H6322H.detail: 1. Pul refers to either a region or a people located in Africa, often identified with Put (ancient Libya). This name appears in a list of lands and peoples that God calls to hear the Gospel, alongside Tarshish, Lud, Tubal, and Javan — regions known to the ancients (Isaiah 66:19). It is a distant land that had never heard of God and to which the survivors of Israel must bring the good news.
H6322H.origine: The word Pul is a proper noun whose original meaning is "distinguishing" (that which is distinguished). It serves as a variant or another name for Put, a region in North Africa. In the biblical context, it represents the distant and pagan peoples that God desires to reach through the testimony of His people.
H6322H.emploi: Pul appears only once in the Bible in Isaiah 66:19, in a final prophetic vision. The prophet lists the nations to which God will send the survivors of Israel to proclaim His glory. These peoples, including Pul, had never heard the Gospel. This mention is part of God's missionary purpose: to make His glory known to all peoples, even the most distant and least touched by divine revelation. Thus, Pul represents a peripheral people destined to receive the biblical testimony.
H6322H.portee: This verse reminds believers that God wants to be known by all peoples, without exception. No people is too distant, no region too forgotten. The Lord entrusts His children with the mission of proclaiming His glory among the most distant nations. This speaks to every Christian about the urgency of universal testimony.

sens: To be perplexed, disoriented
To have a troubled or disturbed mind
H6323.detail:
1. To be perplexed or disoriented: the word describes a state of mental confusion, as if one no longer knows where they stand. The psalmist who cries "I am troubled" expresses his distress in the face of God's terrors that have overwhelmed him since his youth (Psalms 88:16).
2. To have a troubled mind: it also conveys the idea of a soul shaken, disturbed by intense events or emotions. The troubled seeks to regain footing, to find clarity and assurance.
H6323.origine: The Hebrew root פּוּן (pun) originally evokes the idea of turning or diverting, as if one were turned away from their path or balance. It belongs to a small family of Hebrew words expressing disarray or distraction. The verb is rare in the Bible, making its exact meaning somewhat uncertain for us.
H6323.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 88:16. It is found in the context of intense lamentation: the psalmist expresses his misfortune, his feeling of being burdened by divine terrors since youth, and he uses the word "troubled" to describe the state of his mind in the face of this accumulation of suffering.
H6323.portee: This word speaks to those who know the weight of disarray or spiritual anxiety. It shows that the Bible recognizes and names these states of deep disturbance of the soul. For the believer, it is also an invitation: the psalmist lays his troubles before God Himself, suggesting that our confusions and anxieties can become the subject of honest prayer.

sens: Descendants of Puva, son of Issachar
H6324.detail: 1. The Puvites are the members of the clan that descend from Puva (also called Puah), one of the four sons of Issachar. They thus form a family or tribe in the genealogy of Israel.
H6324.origine: The word comes from the proper name Puva (Puah in Hebrew), which means "who divides" or "who disperses." This son of Issachar gave his name to all his descendants, according to the biblical custom of forming clan names from the patronym of the founder.
H6324.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:23, during the census of the Israelites after the desert of Sinai. It is at this time that Moses enumerates the families of Issachar, and the Puvites are mentioned as one of the four major branches of the Issachar clan, alongside the Tolaites, the Jashubites, and the Shimronites.

sens: Desert station where Israel camped during the Exodus
H6325.detail: 1. Punon is a camping place on the route of the Exodus, located in the desert between the Red Sea and the Promised Land. Israel established its camp there after leaving Tzalmonah and before arriving at Oboth (Numbers 33:42-43). It was one of the many stops on the long forty-year journey leading the people from Egypt to Canaan.
H6325.origine: The name Punon, according to its Hebrew root, evokes darkness or gloom (from the root meaning "to be dark"). This interpretation may reflect the arid and inhospitable nature of the place, or a geographical feature noted by the ancients. The name remains without certain etymology, but it designates a specific locality in the Negev, the semi-desert region of southern the Promised Land.
H6325.emploi: Punon appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the passage of Numbers 33 that enumerates the forty-two stations of the people of Israel in the desert. This passage is an itinerary summary of the Exodus journey, and each site is mentioned as a landmark of the divine journey. Punon is a simple stop among many others, with no particular event reported, which shows that the text is concerned here with documenting the route rather than recounting exploits.

sens: Woman, Hebrew midwife during the time of Moses and slavery in Egypt
H6326.detail: Pua is one of the two Hebrew midwives mentioned in Exodus. She and her companion Shiphrah were ordered by Pharaoh to kill all the boys born to the Hebrews (Exodus 1:15). These two women refused to obey this cruel order, fearing God rather than the king, and allowed the male children to live. They represent an act of courage and moral conscience in the face of unjust tyranny.
H6326.origine: The name Pua means "splendid" or "brilliant" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking brightness and light. This name, although borne by only one woman in the Bible, embodies a woman of character — she who chose to illuminate life rather than destroy it, despite the orders of power.
H6326.emploi: Pua appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 1:15, where she is named alongside Shiphrah as a midwife of the Hebrews in Egypt. She has no other mentions or later role in the biblical narrative. Her importance lies entirely in this act of obedience to God rather than to human orders, at the critical moment of the persecution of the Hebrews under Pharaoh. Her story is brief but profound: she embodies silent resistance to injustice.
H6326.portee: The example of Pua teaches that moral courage consists of obeying God even when human authority commands injustice. It shows that acts of faithfulness, even the most humble and hidden, matter to God. Her refusal to participate in the murder of innocent children reminds us that the Christian conscience must prevail over the orders of the powerful, and that God honors those who fear Him more than men.

sens: To be scattered, to separate in different places
To send something or someone in various directions so that it spreads
To chase away, to put to flight and separate a group of people
To spread a substance or influence so that it extends
H6327A.detail:
1. To be scattered, to separate in different places: this is the natural situation where a gathered group divides and moves away. In 1 Samuel 11:11, after the battle against the Ammonites, the defeated enemies "were dispersed," meaning that each fled in their own direction, and "there were not two left together."

2. To send something or someone in various directions so that it spreads: this is the action of an agent that causes this separation. God says in Jeremiah 9:16: "I will disperse them among nations that neither they nor their fathers have known" — He will be the one who sends them to spread throughout the world as punishment.

3. To chase away, to put to flight and separate a group of people: the image is that of a pursuit that breaks apart a troop. In Job 18:11, terrors "pursue" the wicked, overwhelm them, and disperse them on all sides.

4. To spread a substance or influence so that it extends: the word also describes how one sows seeds or spreads a material. In Isaiah 28:25, the plowman and the sower "disperse" the seeds on the ground so that they spread evenly.
H6327A.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the movement of scattering in all directions, like a cloud or a swarm that disseminates. The family word always denotes this idea of separation and extension in space. It is a very biblical verb, very present in the vocabulary of the Old Testament, especially in the prophets to describe how God disperses Israel in exile among the nations.
H6327A.emploi: This verb occurs 61 times in the Old Testament and is especially found in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah) and in national history (Samuel, Kings). It primarily describes the natural flight of a defeated or attacked group: the enemies scattered in war, the Canaanite families who disperse to colonize the land (Genesis 10:18). But above all, it describes the divine action of dispersion: God disperses Israel among the nations as punishment for unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:64, Jeremiah 9:16, Ezekiel 36:19). The verb is also a promise: God "will gather those whom He has dispersed" (Ezekiel 11:17), which expresses both judgment and the hope of restoration. In poetry, the word also describes how God "spreads" His judgment in a storm or how the stars are "scattered" in the sky (Job 37:11).
H6327A.portee: This word reveals the reality of Israel's exile as a voluntary dispersion by God, punishment indeed, but with a purpose of conversion and final restoration. For the believer, it reminds us that no flight or separation escapes divine control, and that even the judgment of dispersion is inscribed in sacred history. It is also an invitation to trust: one who feels scattered, distant from their homeland or people, knows that God can gather them.

sens: One who disperses, who sows desolation
One who destroys, who ruins a city or a people
Figure of the enemy who ravages and devastates
H6327B.detail: 1. The word literally designates someone who scatters, who disperses — like throwing grains to the wind. In Nahum 2:2, the "destroyer" advances against the city of Nineveh: it is the enemy army that sows death and ruin in its path. 2. More broadly, it refers to one who destroys, who annihilates. The prophet Nahum uses it to describe the assailant who will overturn the fortifications and demolish the defenses of the Assyrian capital. 3. The image evokes an unrelenting ravager, one who leaves nothing standing in their wake — which Nahum uses to depict the inevitable and terrifying invasion.
H6327B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to disperse, to scatter, to put to flight." It carries the image of chaos and disorganization: something or someone that sows disorder, that causes flight, that destroys the established order. The prefix "me-" at the beginning designates the agent, the one who performs the action — it literally means "the one who disperses."
H6327B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 2:2, where the prophet uses it to address Judah in the face of the Assyrian threat. Nahum personifies the aggressor (the king of Assyria, Sennacherib or his successor) as the "destroyer" who marches against Nineveh — although it is paradoxical, as Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, will itself be destroyed. The context shows that it is an irresistible enemy, a force of desolation that can only be stopped if one prepares for resistance.
