H6327B.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of destructive evil in the history of peoples: war, invasion, ruin come. But at the same time, Nahum does not address them to frighten — he calls for vigilance and trust in God. For the Christian, it also evokes spiritual vigilance against what can destroy us: passions, lies, the forgetfulness of God.

sens: that which flows or overflows in great quantity
material wealth and prosperity
that which pours out or spreads widely
H6327C.detail: 1. The word first paints the image of something that flows or overflows — the image of a flood. When water is poured into an overflowing container, it spills out and spreads everywhere: it is this flow, this profusion that continues to flow. 2. In the mouth of the Bible, this abundance becomes prosperity and material wealth. In Zechariah 1:17, the Lord promises His cities that they will have "goods in abundance" — not drop by drop, but in a continuous flow, in overflowing generosity. 3. The word also evokes that which spreads, extends widely, without restraint. The image of overflowing and flowing suggests something that does not hold back, that flows generously.
H6327C.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means properly "to flow, to run out." It paints the image of a flood and outpouring. It is a vivid and figurative verb: the choice of this word to speak of wealth shows that the Bible sees prosperity not as a hoarded and closed treasure, but as something fluid, that flows and pours out.
H6327C.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in the cited passages. In Zechariah 1:17, it refers to the future prosperity that God promises to His cities — it is the wealth and well-being that flow generously. Elsewhere, in Proverbs 5:16, the context is that of adultery, where the image of the flood takes on a connotation of wandering and loss. In both cases, the underlying image remains that of overflowing and profusion.
H6327C.portee: This word invites the believer to see divine blessing not as a stingy and measured distribution, but as a flood, a generosity that flows and pours out. The promise in Zechariah reminds us that God does not give drop by drop: He fills abundantly. This encourages trust in His inexhaustible generosity.

sens: To break, to reduce to pieces
To strike violently to destroy
To annihilate the resistance or integrity of something
H6327D.detail:
1. To break means to reduce something to fragments, to shatter it violently. It is a concrete physical destruction: the rock that is broken with a hammer splits into shards (Jeremiah 23:29).
2. The word evokes an act of violence that strikes and pulverizes: the image is that of a sharp and destructive blow, like when one delivers a hammer strike (Jeremiah 23:29).
3. Broken can also describe a moral or spiritual state: to be broken is to have lost one's integrity, strength, or unity — Job says he has been seized and broken by his misfortune (Job 16:12).
H6327D.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּצַץ comes from a root that expresses the idea of fragmenting, of reducing to shards. The forms used in the Bible are intensive: they reinforce the image of violent and complete destruction. The word belongs to the vocabulary of destructive force, whether physical or moral.
H6327D.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Segond. In Job 16:12, Job complains that God has broken him — seized and destroyed like an adversary — during his trial: the word describes a physical and moral violence that annihilates. In Jeremiah 23:29, the Lord compares His word to a hammer that breaks the rock: here, to break illustrates the irresistible power of God's word, which can destroy all resistance. In both cases, the verb emphasizes total and definitive destruction.
H6327D.portee: Understanding that to break describes the powerful action of God helps to grasp the strength of His word: it does not merely persuade, it transforms and destroys what opposes it. This can also shed light on suffering when one feels broken by life: the biblical word names this reality without denying it, inviting us not to minimize the destruction that a believer goes through, but to believe that God remains master of what seems irreparably broken.

sens: To lose balance, to sway from side to side
To be unstable, to move unsteadily
Staggering of a drunken or sick person
H6328.detail:
1. The word describes the physical movement of one who loses balance and sways: it is the image of a body that tilts first to one side, then to the other, without stability. In Isaiah 28:7, the priests and prophets who are intoxicated "stagger" — they can no longer stand upright, drunk on wine and strong drink.
2. More broadly, to stagger means to be unstable, to move without solidity. An object that wobbles, like the idol in Jeremiah 10:4 that must be secured with nails so it does not "wobble," is an object that does not hold its place, threatening to fall or shift.
3. Applied to a person, this verb highlights the collapse of judgment and wisdom: the prophets and priests in Isaiah can no longer discern or render justice because alcohol makes them stagger — both their mind and body lose grip.
H6328.origine: The Hebrew verb puq expresses the idea of unstable and oscillating movement. It belongs to a family of words that describe the absence of firmness and lost balance. The basic image is that of a body or object that does not hold firmly, that sways or stumbles.
H6328.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 28:7, it depicts the priests and prophets of Israel who stagger under the influence of wine and strong drink, unable to render clear judgments or prophesy correctly — their intoxication makes them morally and spiritually unstable. In Jeremiah 10:4, the same verb (here "wobble") describes the pagan idol that must be secured with nails to prevent it from moving — an image of vanity: unlike the living God, the idol is so fragile that it must be immobilized to stand upright.
H6328.portee: This word reminds the believer that alcohol and substances that disturb the mind deprive them of clarity to serve God and His people. More broadly, it invites us to examine anything that may destabilize our walk with the Lord: what makes us stagger in faith, judgment, or righteousness deserves to be identified and rejected. It is a call to sobriety and steadfastness of heart.

sens: To bring out, to produce, to reveal
To come to have, to acquire in return
To allow something to happen or to manifest
H6329.detail:
1. To bring out, to produce, to reveal: the word evokes the idea of making something emerge that was hidden or held back. In Psalms 144:13, the granaries "overflow" with provisions: it is the same root, which shows an abundance that flows and manifests outward. The concrete sense is that of production or bringing to light.
2. To come to have, to acquire in return: this is the most common sense in Proverbs. He who finds wisdom "possesses" understanding (Proverbs 3:13), he who finds divine Wisdom "obtains" life and favor from the Lord (Proverbs 8:35). It is a result that one acquires, often as a happy consequence of a search or action.
3. To allow something to happen or to manifest: this is the sense of promotion or production. In Psalms 140:9, not fulfilling the desires of the wicked "for fear" that he may boast: it is to prevent a situation from manifesting or developing.
H6329.origine: The Hebrew root puq means to bring out, to produce. It belongs to the family of verbs of movement and production. The verb is mainly used in the intensive form (Hiphil), which intensifies the idea: not only does something come out, but it is actively brought out, produced, generated. This form is one of effectiveness and causality.
H6329.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms and Proverbs, and once in Isaiah 58:10. In Proverbs, it describes what one acquires as the fruit of an action or encounter: finding wisdom allows one to "obtain" life, finding a wife is a grace that one "obtains" from the Lord. The word then expresses a reward, a blessing that results. In Psalms, the sense is similar: overflowing abundance, prosperity that manifests. Only once, in Psalms 140:9, does it take on a negative nuance: not fulfilling (or allowing to succeed) a malicious desire.
H6329.portee: This word teaches that access to divine blessings — wisdom, favor from God, prosperity — is not by chance: it is obtained, it is earned, it comes as a natural fruit of the right search or action. For the believer, it is a call to actively seek wisdom and favor from God, knowing that he will "obtain" them in return. The word also reminds us that all good comes from the hand of the Lord: we possess nothing of our own, we receive and obtain by grace.

sens: Staggering, wavering of the body
Conscience trouble, guilt
Painful regret for a wrong action
H6330.detail:
1. The word literally designates the action of staggering, losing balance — like someone who stumbles or wavers on their legs.
2. The Bible transposes this physical image to the realm of conscience: remorse is when the conscience 'wavers' before a committed fault, an inner turmoil that destabilizes. In 1 Samuel 25:31, Abigail asks King David that his conscience not be troubled by the regret of having shed blood unnecessarily — she wants to spare him from the remorse that would 'make him stagger.'
3. The word thus expresses this bitter regret, this gnawing guilt that shakes the soul after a wrong action.
H6330.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of wavering, losing footing. It first evokes physical instability — the body that staggers — and has been used figuratively to describe the instability of the conscience troubled by guilt. It is a striking image: sin makes inner peace 'stagger.'
H6330.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 25:31. Abigail, a wise and pious woman, intercedes with King David to spare him from remorse (from this agitation of conscience) if he were to shed blood unnecessarily in seeking revenge. She recognizes that personal vengeance leaves a wound on the soul — remorse — and she preserves David by proposing a better way. The context shows that this word describes the inner weight of guilt, more than just a fleeting emotion.
H6330.portee: This word reminds us that sin affects not only our actions but our conscience. Remorse is the signal that something has broken within us — a suffering of the soul that shows we have violated our convictions. For the believer, remorse can become an opportunity for sincere repentance and reconciliation with God and others.

sens: Break, shatter something material
Destroy, annihilate a project, a plan
Violate, transgress a commitment or covenant
H6331.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to break or shatter an object. It is the action of destroying the solidity of something.
2. Figuratively, the word applies to plans and designs: to overturn means to annihilate them, to render them ineffective. God 'overturns the plans of nations' (Psalms 33:10), meaning He destroys them or prevents them from succeeding.
3. The word is also used for commitments and covenants: to 'break' them means to transgress, to violate, to declare them null. When one 'breaks' a covenant (Ezekiel 17:19), one rejects it and no longer respects its conditions.
H6331.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the image of breaking and destruction. The verb has a meaning close to that of par (פָּרַר), which also means 'to break' or 'to annihilate.' These two words express the idea of reducing something to nothing, whether physical or moral.
H6331.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament. In Psalms 33:10, it describes the divine action that overturns the plans that nations project — God intervenes to destroy them. In Psalms 89:34, it evokes the possibility (that God dismisses) of breaking His covenant. In Ezekiel 17:19, it concerns a violation of covenant by a man: the oath and commitment made in God's name are despised and broken. The word consistently retains the idea of destruction or annulment.
H6331.portee: This word reveals God's power over all human plans: no project of nations can stand against His will. It also shows the solemn importance of covenants and promises before God — breaking them is not a light act, but a serious transgression that brings His judgment.

sens: Object or method for deciding by chance
Decision made by drawing lots
The Jewish festival of Purim, which commemorates the deliverance of the Jews from Haman's plot
H6332.detail: 1. The word pur primarily designates an object or method for letting chance decide a question: lots (like dice or tokens) are cast to know the outcome. Haman used this method to determine the month and day of his attempted massacre of the Jews (Esther 3:7). 2. By extension, pur means the decision itself, the result of the drawing, which becomes the fate or will expressed by the lot. This determines events: in the case of Haman's plot, the lot he cast was meant to bring death to the Jews (Esther 9:24). 3. The word has given its name to the festival of Purim (Purim in Hebrew), which the Jews celebrate each year to remember how God delivered them from Haman's murderous scheme, thus transforming the lot cast for their destruction into an occasion of joy and victory (Esther 9:26, 9:28).
H6332.origine: The Hebrew word pur comes from a root meaning 'piece' or 'part' — that is, an element that is separated or divided for drawing lots. Its etymology refers to the concrete gesture of drawing lots by fragments. The word has specialized to designate the festival instituted in memory of the miraculous deliverance, whose name perpetuates the only visible human instrument of Haman's plot: his casting of lots.
H6332.emploi: The word pur appears seven times in the book of Esther, exclusively in chapter 9 and in Esther 3:7. It always refers to the lot cast by Haman to choose the time for the extermination of the Jews. The early uses (Esther 3:7 and 9:24) describe the concrete gesture: the pur was cast 'for each day and for each month.' The following passages (Esther 9:26, 9:28, 9:29, 9:31, 9:32) explain the institution of the festival of Purim, which received its name from this lot. The context is always the miraculous deliverance and the reversal of Haman's plot: what was destined for death became an occasion for celebration and deliverance.
H6332.portee: This word invites the believer to see how God governs events that seem left to chance. Haman's casting of lots appeared decisive in his eyes, but God turned this murderous plan into an occasion for salvation. It is a reminder that no lot, no human malice can thwart God's plan for His people: He remains sovereign, even in appearances of chance.

sens: Installation or basin where grapes are trodden to extract juice
Measure of capacity for liquids
H6333.detail:
1. The winepress is the pit or basin dug into the rock or built of masonry where the harvesters trod the grapes with their feet to extract the juice and make wine — it is a common element of ancient viticulture. Isaiah uses it as an image of divine judgment: the Lord treads the peoples as one treads grapes, and their 'blood' gushes out like the juice of the winepress (Isaiah 63:3).
2. The word also designates a unit of measure for volume for liquids. In Haggai 2:16, when the harvest has failed, people came hoping to draw fifty measures of wine from the winepress, but found only twenty: the term 'measure' translates the same Hebrew word here, indicating the quantity that the winepress should contain or produce.
H6333.origine: The Hebrew word purah comes from the root par, which means 'to tread' or 'to press.' The same root appears in other words related to pressing and treading. The image is that of the physical action of treading: the feet crush and press to extract the liquid. In Greek, this term is rendered by lenos or lemna.
H6333.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 63:3, it carries its primary and concrete meaning: the winepress is the installation where grapes are trodden. Isaiah makes it a powerful image of the final judgment, where God alone treads the sinful nations as one treads grapes. In Haggai 2:16, the same word takes on the meaning of a measure of capacity, since the winepress is the place where wine was harvested and measured; the poor harvest means that the expected measures cannot be filled. These two uses, concrete and metric, reveal how a word gains meaning through logical extension.
H6333.portee: The winepress of Isaiah 63 profoundly marks Christian faith: it symbolizes the inevitable and solar divine judgment, where the Lord acts alone to crush evil and rebellion. This image helps the believer understand the extent of God's wrath, but also His solitude and determination. It is a key image of the end times and God's final victory.

sens: One of the ten sons of the wicked Haman
H6334.detail: Poratha is a minor character in the book of Esther, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian vizier who conspires to destroy all the Jews in the empire (Esther 9:8). Poratha and his brothers are executed during the Jews' vengeance against the enemies of Mordecai and Esther, in accordance with the decree that the king had initially granted to Haman to annihilate them.
H6334.origine: The name Poratha comes from Hebrew and means "abundance" or "fertility." It carries an auspicious name, but his story shows the irony of fate: destined to prosper, he perishes along with his entire family. It is a Persian name adapted to the time and context of the narrative.
H6334.emploi: Poratha appears only in the book of Esther, in chapter 9, verse 8. He is named among the ten sons of Haman who are hanged on the day when the Jews defend themselves against their enemies in Susa, the Persian capital. His name is simply listed among the slain sons, without any personal characteristics specified. This event marks the complete reversal of Haman's fate and the salvation of the Jewish people.
H6334.portee: The fate of Poratha and his brothers reminds us that God overturns the plans of the wicked and protects His people. Although Poratha is just a name in a list, his fate illustrates the spectacular reversal that God works in history: those who sought the annihilation of the Jews perish themselves.

sens: To jump, to leap with vigor and lightness
To show pride or arrogance through haughty gestures
H6335A.detail:
1. The word describes the action of jumping, making vigorous and light leaps. It is the natural movement of a young and vigorous animal expressing its strength and energy. In Malachi 4:2, believers who fear God "shall leap like calves from the stall," the image evoking the overflowing joy and exuberance of one who has just been liberated.
2. Figuratively, to leap expresses pride and arrogance — one who shows haughtiness "leaps" with malicious pride. In Habakkuk 1:8, the enemy horsemen "advance with pride," their horses' leaps reflecting a dominating and threatening pride; in Jeremiah 50:11, Babylon "leaps" in the wicked joy of having plundered God's people, exulting in its conquering arrogance.
H6335A.origine: The Hebrew verb פּוּשׁ (push) fundamentally expresses the image of jumping and leaping — the lively and energetic movement of a creature that has strength and life. This concrete image of the body rising and bouncing naturally becomes the sign of intense feelings: exuberant joy or triumphant pride. It is a specific root for vehement jumping, distinct from other Hebrew verbs for jumping.
H6335A.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, each time in an emotionally charged context. In Jeremiah 50:11, it is Babylon that "leaps" with wicked joy in celebrating the plundering of Israel — a pride that God will condemn. In Habakkuk 1:8, the horses of the invaders leap forward, their violence reflecting the arrogance of those who ride them. In Malachi 4:2, the same verb is turned into a promise of joy: the righteous who fear God "shall leap" at the coming of the sun of righteousness, expressing the liberating joy of one whom God saves. The word changes moral color according to the heart of the one who leaps.
H6335A.portee: This verb teaches that joy and pride are expressed in the body — our gestures reveal our heart. For the believer, "leaping" is not a shame: it is the legitimate expression of the joy that God gives to those who fear Him and receive His righteousness. But it also warns us: haughty exultation and conquering pride are symptoms of a heart far from God, and God does not leave unpunished those who leap in mockery of His people.

sens: To be scattered, separated and spread out in different places
To spread without order or connection
To be unprotected, abandoned without guidance
H6335B.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a crowd or group that no longer holds together, that crumbles and scatters to the four winds. In Nahum 3:18, the Assyrian people, once their leaders no longer guide them, disperse on the mountains like cattle without a shepherd.
2. Beyond simple physical separation, the word suggests a loss of order and coherence: what was united fragments, spreads without direction. This happens to an army or a nation when it loses its leaders.
3. The dispersion also carries the idea of abandonment and vulnerability: the people scattered on the mountains have no one to gather them (Nahum 3:18), they are exposed, unprotected, left to themselves.
H6335B.origine: The Hebrew word פּוּשׁ (push) expresses the idea of spreading out, scattering. In its Niphal form (the one used here), it marks a passive state: it is not the subject that chooses to disperse, but it is dispersed, it finds itself scattered. It is a strong image of disintegration and loss of cohesion, often linked to the absence of direction or the ruin of a community.
H6335B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Nahum which announces the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. In Nahum 3:18, it describes the Assyrian people in full debacle: deprived of their shepherds (their kings and generals), they disperse on the mountains. This passage from Nahum is a prophecy of divine judgment; the dispersion of the people is the visible sign of their political and military collapse.
H6335B.portee: This word reminds us that the absence of true direction leads to the dissolution of a people and to its misfortune. For the believer, it also emphasizes the importance of a sure guide and a united community. The dispersion is presented as a curse, the opposite of what God desires for His people: unity and protection under just authority.

sens: Members of a family of Judah
H6336.detail: 1. The Puthiens are a family descended from Judah, mentioned in the genealogical register of God's people. They are listed among the families of Kirjath-Jearim, alongside the Jethrites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites (1 Chronicles 2:53).
H6336.origine: This name designates the descendants of an ancestor named Puth, whose biblical genealogies have preserved the memory. The name belongs to the structure of the genealogies of Judah and represents one of the family branches of God's people, recorded in the history of Israel.
H6336.emploi: The Puthiens are mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:53, in the context of the genealogies of the people of Judah. This passage lists the families of Kirjath-Jearim, a city in the Negev or the hills of Judah. Although little documented, they constitute a recognized part of Israel's genealogical heritage, alongside the other families listed.

sens: Refined gold, free from any impurity
Material of great value, symbol of purity and preciousness
H6337.detail:
1. The word refers to gold after refining, the purest gold possible. It is the gold desired in precious objects: without alloy, without mixture of inferior metal. When the psalmist says that God's commandments are more precious than fine gold (Psalms 119:127), he evokes the extreme purity and invaluable rarity of this material.
2. Figuratively, fine gold represents everything that has the highest value and greatest purity. Wisdom, as a fruit of righteousness, produces something better than pure gold (Proverbs 8:19): it is not just good, it is untainted good, authentic good. Similarly, the crown of pure gold placed on the king's head (Psalms 21:4) symbolizes a power adorned with pure dignity.
H6337.origine: The word paz refers to gold after it has gone through the fire of refining. Its image is that of purity obtained through trial and the separation of base elements. It is a classic Hebrew word to express the supreme quality of gold, distinct from ordinary or mixed gold. The context of its uses always ties it to realities that the biblical text places above any earthly value.
H6337.emploi: The word paz appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom and poetic books. It is used when the text wants to convey that something is not only precious but of unparalleled purity and value. The psalms and proverbs use it to express the incomparable superiority of God's word and wisdom over all earthly riches. In the Song of Solomon (5:11 and 5:15), fine gold describes the beauty of the beloved, adorned with immaculate splendor. Isaiah (13:12) and Lamentations (4:2) use it in contexts of absolute rarity, emphasizing that even fine gold becomes rarer than men in the eyes of God.
H6337.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on true value. God places His commandments and His wisdom above fine gold — the purest good one can imagine on earth. This calls for discerning what truly matters: not corruptible riches, even the purest, but the word of God, which alone has a value that surpasses all. It is a call to the hierarchy of values in Christ.

sens: Refined, purified, free from impurities
Shining with purity
Without mixture, of integral quality
H6338.detail: 1. The word first describes what has been refined, purified, free from everything that alters or sullies it — like gold that has undergone fire to be purified. In 1 Kings 10:18, the royal throne that King Solomon had covered with pure gold shows that it is refined gold, shining, without alloy: the highest quality gold, worthy of a king. 2. The word also carries the idea of a radiant purity: what is pure shines, it is not tarnished. 3. By extension, being pure means being integral, without mixture, without compromise — a moral quality as well as a material one.
H6338.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of refining, purifying by fire or treatment. It is the idea of precious metal going through the crucible to be separated from all impure mixture. The form used here (Hophal) marks the result: something that IS pure, that HAS BEEN refined. This root connects with the biblical imagery of fire that purifies and purity as beauty and integrity.
H6338.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament (translated in French as "pure"), and it refers to the pure gold of Solomon's royal throne. The context is that of royal magnificence: Solomon builds a throne of ivory, a symbol of power, which he covers with refined gold, the most beautiful and precious. This choice shows that the author emphasizes the supreme quality, the absolute purity of the materials: it is the expression of the glory and honor of the king of Israel. The solitary use of the word suggests that biblical Hebrew resorted to other more common terms to express purity.
H6338.portee: This word reminds us that purity, in the Bible, is not a cold moral abstraction: it is associated with beauty, integrity, and dignity. The pure gold of Solomon's throne evokes how God desires us to be purified, not out of vanity, but to shine with the light of His righteousness. It is an invitation to allow God to refine us in the crucible of faith, like gold in the fire, so that our lives reflect His purity and brilliance.

sens: To jump, to spring with agility
To dance or move lively before God
H6339.detail:
1. To leap means to jump, to make quick and agile movements of the body. It is the image of a person or an animal leaving the ground, springing up. In the biblical context, this describes David leaping and dancing before the Ark of the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16).
2. The word can also express expressive joy and freedom of movement, particularly in a religious celebration. When David leaps before the Ark, it is an act of joyful devotion, a way to publicly manifest his delight in God.
H6339.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּזַז (pazaz) expresses the fundamental idea of lively and agile movement, of repeated leaps. It belongs to a family of words that describe the liveliness and agility of the body. The starting image is that of lightness and suppleness, like an animal leaping effortlessly. This word reflects a dynamic and energetic vision of movement.
H6339.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence is found in Genesis 49:24, in the context of strength and vigor. The second, in 2 Samuel 6:16, shows David leaping and dancing before the Ark of the Covenant with overflowing joy. These two uses reveal that the word serves to describe energetic and free movement, either as an expression of physical strength or as a manifestation of religious joy. The context of 2 Samuel 6 is particularly significant: King David, dressed in the priestly garment, leaps before the Ark with abandon, provoking the disdain of Michal, his wife, who judges him unworthy.
H6339.portee: For the reader, this word invites understanding that authentic joy before God can be manifested through visible and free gestures, without restraint. David's example shows that dance and leap are not incompatible with deep devotion to the Lord. This challenges everything that seeks to stifle or shame the enthusiastic expression of faith.

sens: Scatter, separate in different places
Spread, pour out abundantly
Dislocate, put into disorder
Be dispersed, fragment
H6340.detail:
1. Dispersing means scattering something or someone in space. It is the image of what was gathered and is now separating, disseminating. In Esther 3:8, the Jews are described as "dispersed" among the provinces of the Persian kingdom, forming a separated people amidst other peoples.
2. The word also refers to the action of generously spreading, particularly when talking about gifts or generosity. Psalms 112:9 states that the one who "disperses" gives to the needy, an image of someone who lets their generosity flow in all directions like pouring out grain.
3. Dispersing can mean breaking, dislocating the order or cohesion of an army or gathering. Psalms 89:11 mentions how God "dispersed" His enemies by the power of His arm, meaning He put them to flight, defeated them.
4. In the passive form, the word describes the state of what is dispersed, fragmented. Psalms 141:7 speaks of the bones dispersed at the entrance of the abode of the dead, an image of violent death and the dismemberment of the body.
H6340.origine: The root פזר (p.z.r) evokes the action of separating and scattering. It appears in several grammatical forms to express either the action of actively dispersing or the resulting state of being dispersed. The word belongs to the vocabulary of separation and division, without intrinsic moral connotation: depending on the context, it can describe divine punishment, the generous action of a liberal heart, or simply a material fact.
H6340.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible. In the Psalms and historical narratives, it primarily describes a destructive action: God or a king disperses enemies, defeating them by putting them to flight (Psalms 53:6, 89:11, Psalms 147:16 for nature spreading snow). In the prophets Jeremiah and Joel, it evokes the exile and dispersion of the people as punishment. But in Psalms 112:9 and Proverbs 11:24, it takes on a positive tone: the one who "disperses" their goods, that is, who gives generously, does not become impoverished but is enriched in blessing. The word can thus convey both violence and liberality.
H6340.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God controls the dispersion and gathering of peoples, and that He can transform a suffered dispersion into an opportunity for testimony. It also shows that true wealth consists in "dispersing" one's goods to the poor, not hoarding them selfishly: giving generously is an act of faith in divine providence.

sens: Net or snare to capture birds
Danger, obstacle, or situation from which one cannot escape
Calamity, punishment, or misfortune that befalls someone
Ruse or trap intentionally set by adversaries
H6341A.detail:
1. A trap is primarily a net or hunting device intended to capture live birds — it is the concrete image of the word. Amos 3:5 asks: "Does a bird fall into a trap on the ground, when there is no bird that has set it?" — the image of the hunter setting his net.

2. The word extends to any inevitable danger from which one cannot escape: a situation that ensnares you like a net. Job 18:9 speaks of the wicked: "A net seizes him by the feet, and he rushes into a pit." The trap metaphorically becomes anything that captures and ruins you.

3. Applied to divine punishment or calamity, the trap is the misfortune that strikes — less as a ruse than as inevitability. Psalms 11:6: "He rains coals [a trap of fire], fire and brimstone upon the wicked" — judgment as an inescapable capture.

4. The trap can also refer to the ruse or ambush that adversaries intentionally set. Psalms 119:110: "The wicked lay traps for me" — here, it is the conscious and malevolent plot. Jeremiah 18:22 reports: "They have dug a pit to swallow me and have set traps for me" — the human, malevolent trap.
H6341A.origine: The Hebrew word pach comes from a root that evokes the action of setting or extending a net. It literally designates the trap of the hunter — the device spread out to capture birds. From there, the image of the trap naturally extends to danger, misfortune, and ambush: anything that, like a net, ensnares and captures a being with no possibility of escape. It is a very vivid word in the Hebrew Bible, where the trap serves to express both divine judgment and the ruses of the wicked.
H6341A.emploi: The word pach appears twenty-three times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms (about ten occurrences), Proverbs, and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea). It primarily designates the literal trap of the hunter (Amos 3:5, Ecclesiastes 9:12), but the majority of uses transform it into an image of spiritual and moral danger. In the Psalms, the psalmist implores God to deliver him from the traps of his enemies: "Deliver me from the trap they have laid for me" (Psalms 141:9). In Proverbs, the trap symbolizes the ruses of evil: "Thorns and snares are in the way of the perverse man" (Proverbs 22:5). In the prophets, the trap becomes the judgment of God: Isaiah 24:17 lists "terror, pit, and net" as the three forms of punishment that come. The word thus changes nuance: sometimes human ruse, sometimes divine calamity, but always the image of an inevitable capture.
H6341A.portee: This word reminds the biblical reader that evil — whether human ruse or divine judgment — functions like a trap: one falls into it and cannot escape alone. It calls for spiritual vigilance ("keep your soul," says Proverbs 22:5) and trust in God for deliverance. The Psalms depict the trap as the weapon of the wicked and the believer's call for divine protection: it is a concrete image of the invisible battle of faith.

sens: Thin sheet of hammered and stretched metal
Coating or plating of metal for an altar or a sacred object
H6341B.detail:
1. A blade is a thin sheet of metal, obtained by hammering and stretching the metal to make it very thin. In Exodus 39:3, gold is transformed into fine blades, then cut into threads that are woven into the garments of the high priest: it is luxurious and meticulous decorative work.
2. A blade can also refer to a plating or coating of metal intended to cover a structure, particularly a cult object. In Numbers 16:38, the bronze censers of the rebels are transformed into stretched blades to cover the altar of the Lord: this covering becomes a visible reminder of God's judgment and the holiness of the altar.
H6341B.origine: The Hebrew word pach designates the work of beaten and stretched metal. The image comes from the verb that means "to stretch" or "to hammer": the metal is literally flattened and stretched by the work of the blacksmith or artisan. It is a technical term in the vocabulary of the crafts and the construction of Israelite worship.
H6341B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in contexts related to the Tabernacle and its ornaments. In Exodus 39, it refers to the fine decoration of the priestly garment, where gold is transformed into very fine blades. In Numbers 16, the censers of the rebels (Korah and his company) are converted into metal blades to cover the altar: an act that sanctifies the object and makes it a lasting sign of divine judgment. Both uses highlight the transformation of raw metal into an element of worship.
H6341B.portee: This word reminds us that everything in the worship of God requires work, finesse, and careful craftsmanship. The gold blades of the priest's garment and the blades of the altar symbolize the beauty and holiness that characterize the approach to God. The work of the artisan becomes a form of testimony: through these blades, we see the glory of God and the importance of how we serve Him.

sens: To be afraid, to feel fear in the face of danger or threat
To physically shudder, to tremble all over due to fear
To experience respectful fear, dread before God or His power
To greatly dread something, to be anxious about it
H6342.detail:
1. To be afraid or fearful: this is to feel fear in the face of danger. When the princes persecute the psalmist without cause, his heart trembles "only at your words" (Psalms 119:161), meaning that only the Word of God inspires a fear that truly matters.
2. To physically shudder or tremble: the body reacts to fear with involuntary shivers and shakes. In Isaiah 44:11, the idolatrous workers are described as "trembling," shaken by shame and dread before the impotence of their gods.
3. Respectful fear or holy fear before God: this is a form of reverence mixed with sacred dread. In Psalms 14:5, the wicked "will tremble with terror when God appears among the righteous." 
4. To dread, to apprehend with anxiety: this is a constant concern, a distress. In Deuteronomy 28:66, the one living under the curse "will tremble night and day, and will doubt his existence," living in chronic fear.
H6342.origine: The Hebrew verb pachad primarily expresses a physical movement of contraction or shaking: to tremble. This image of the body shaken by fear naturally extends to the inner feeling of fear. The root evokes an instinctive, bodily, and emotional reaction at the same time. The word belongs to the ancient Hebrew emotional vocabulary, where bodily sensations and states of the soul are not separated.
H6342.emploi: The verb pachad appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mostly in Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It denotes either ordinary human fear in the face of enemies or trials (Deuteronomy 28:66-67, Job 3:25), or the sacred fear that arises from the presence or action of God (Psalms 14:5, Isaiah 19:16). In Psalms 27:1 and Isaiah 12:2, which are not included in the cited translations but are part of the references, it is the absence of fear due to trust in God that is affirmed. The word fits both moments of sudden terror and prolonged anxiety. Isaiah 19:16-17 shows how fear can fill an entire people in the face of the manifestation of divine power.
H6342.portee: To recognize that fear is natural, human, and not shameful in itself. But the Bible distinguishes legitimate fear — that which arises from reverential fear before God — from slave fear, which paralyzes and distances one from God. The faithful who "tremble" at the Word of God find stability, while those who dread circumstances live without assurance. This is why the New Testament continually invites us not to fear, for God is with us.

sens: Intense, sudden, and paralyzing fear in the face of real or imagined danger
Deep fear, often mixed with respect before a powerful or fearsome presence
The very object that causes this fear, what is to be feared
Oppressive anxiety that invades the mind and body
H6343.detail:
1. Terror is primarily the physical fear that seizes someone in the face of danger: Job speaks of his flesh that "trembles with dread" that God inspires (Psalms 119:120), showing how terror runs through the entire body and paralyzes it. It is also the panic that grips an army or a people — "the terror of the Lord had seized them" in the cities of Gerar (2 Chronicles 14:13).
2. It can also be a fear mixed with respect before a superhuman power: the word applies to the fear one feels before God or before a feared king. In Genesis 31:42, Jacob refers to "the one whom Isaac fears," thus designating the God of Abraham by the sense of reverence He inspires.
3. Sometimes the word designates the very thing that causes fear — "the object of dread" — as when speaking of "the terror of the Lord" not as a feeling, but as His terrifying presence and action (Isaiah 2:21).
4. Terror can also be a persistent anxiety that resides in someone, like "the fear" that Job dreads every day (Job 3:25): this is no longer a panic attack, but a worry that does not leave him.
H6343.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning fundamentally "to tremble" or "to shudder." This image of shivering and trembling is found throughout the Bible: the one who is afraid trembles, their bones rattle, their flesh shivers. The word belongs to the family of words that describe the agitation of the body in the face of danger or divine power.
H6343.emploi: This word appears nearly 50 times in the Hebrew Bible, very often in the wisdom books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and in historical narratives. It carries nuances depending on the context: it can refer to the fear of an army before the enemy (1 Samuel 11:7), religious terror before God (Psalms 119:120), or dread before a disaster (Isaiah 24:17-18). In deliverance narratives, such as Esther, the terror of Israel's enemies contrasts with the joy of the saved people (Esther 9:2-3). The word often expresses that moment when a superhuman power manifests its strength and freezes those who encounter it.
H6343.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian grasp how the Bible speaks of the presence of God: it can evoke a terror that liberates rather than confines, for "the terror of the Lord" is also the beginning of wisdom and salvation. It also shows that the fear of the Lord is not a foolish panic, but an awareness of His majesty before which one submits. In our lives, recognizing what terrifies us — sin, death, injustice — is already accepting that only God can deliver us from it.

sens: Part of the leg between the hip and the knee
Physical strength and power
Symbol of masculinity or power
H6344.detail:
1. The thigh is the fleshy and muscular part of the leg, between the hip and the knee. It is one of the strongest parts of the human body. In Job 40:12, God describes the thighs of the Behemoth (a mythical creature) as particularly strong and massive: "The sinews of his thighs are intertwined," highlighting the extraordinary physical power of this creature.
2. By extension, the thigh represents strength, vigor, and power. Because the thighs are the seat of muscular strength, they become an image of power in biblical language.
3. In ancient context, the thigh also carries a symbolic weight related to masculinity and male authority: one "girds the loins," one "strikes the thigh" as a sign of pain or distress.
H6344.origine: The Hebrew word פַּחַד comes from a root that denotes what is strong or trembles. The word applies literally to the part of the body most charged with muscular power. In biblical texts, the thigh retains this association between the physical (the part of the body) and the symbolic (strength and authority).
H6344.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 40:12, where it describes the thighs of the Behemoth, a gigantic creature that God shows to Job to remind him that the universe contains forces that infinitely surpass him. The emphasis is on the exceptional muscular strength, which the text describes as "intertwined" with powerful sinews.
H6344.portee: This passage invites the reader to contemplate the power of creation and to recognize the immensity of divine wisdom in the face of extraordinary creatures. It teaches humility: Job, confronted with the evidence of his smallness before the works of God, learns to accept what he cannot understand.

sens: Fear, apprehension in the face of danger or authority
Respect mixed with fear towards God
Religious fear, reverence before the sacred
H6345.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes an ordinary fear or apprehension, a worry in the face of what threatens or harms. In Jeremiah 2:19, the Lord says that the people will know "by bitter experience" the misfortune of having lost the fear of God: it is like losing vigilance in the face of real danger.
2. Fear takes on a deeper dimension when it concerns God: it is not just being afraid of His power, but respecting His holiness and recognizing our dependence on Him. This fear combines respect, reverence, and a certain apprehension before the divine majesty.
3. In the religious context, this word expresses the attitude that the believer should have towards the Lord: a sacred fear, not servile but filled with veneration, which compels obedience and turning away from evil.
H6345.origine: The Hebrew word פַּחְדָּה (pach'dah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of trembling or being seized with fear. It belongs to the family of words describing emotional reactions to power and authority. In Hebrew, this word can be used for either secular fear or religious fear, depending on the context.
H6345.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 2:19. The prophet reproaches the people of Israel for having abandoned God and no longer fearing Him. The absence of fear towards the Lord is presented as the source of the ruin and suffering of the people: it is a direct cause of the punishment that God sends. The fear of God is thus the opposite of unfaithfulness.
H6345.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of God is not a morbid fright, but the foundation of a just and faithful life. Losing the fear of the Lord is to deprive oneself of the restraint that protects us from evil and waywardness. For the believer, regaining or cultivating this fear is to find the path of wisdom and obedience.

sens: Administrative officer of a province or territory, appointed by a king or empire
Military leader or administrator in a system of foreign domination
Magistrate with civil and judicial authority
H6346.detail:
1. The governor is an official appointed by the king to administer a province in his name and collect taxes. Nehemiah is an example of this: King Artaxerxes appointed him governor of the land of Judah for twelve years (Nehemiah 5:14). Ezra also encounters the governors on this side of the river, who represent Persian royal authority (Ezra 8:36).
2. The term often designates military and civil leaders of a colonial empire: in Persian accounts, governors administer provinces alongside satraps, the king's high authorities (Esther 3:12). In Jeremiah's vision, God will break the governors and leaders of Babylon, symbols of enemy power (Jeremiah 51:23).
3. Sometimes the word simply describes a leader with local authority: the governors of the kings of Arabia bring their revenues to King Solomon (1 Kings 10:15), and the prophet Haggai addresses Governor Zerubbabel with the respect due to his office (Haggai 1:1).
H6346.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּחָה likely comes from the Persian administrative vocabulary: it appears mainly in texts relating to Persian domination over Israel (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther). It reflects the bureaucratic organization of the Persian Empire, which divided its territories into provinces governed by appointed officials. This term shows how the Hebrew language borrowed vocabulary from the power that dominated it.
H6346.emploi: The word appears 27 times, almost exclusively in the post-exilic historical books (Nehemiah, Ezra, Esther) and the prophets who spoke of the exile (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Haggai). Its use reflects the political context: when Israel is under foreign domination, governors are figures of authority, sometimes respectable (Nehemiah justly administering Judah), sometimes threatening (the Assyrian governors who came to besiege Jerusalem in 2 Kings 18:24). The word is also used for the military and political leaders of Babylon, always as symbols of earthly power that God can bring down.
H6346.portee: The governor represents established and recognized human power: in the New Testament, this Greek and Hebrew vocabulary will later evoke the governor Pontius Pilate. For the exiled Jews, this figure reminds them that God can give wisdom and integrity to a leader, as He did for Nehemiah, and that all earthly power remains subject to God's purposes.

sens: official appointed by the king to administer a province or region
H6347.detail: 1. A governor is a high official whom the king places at the head of a province to govern in his name. He is a man of authority who represents the central power to the local population. In the book of Ezra, Tattenai acts as governor of the territory "on this side of the river" (the Euphrates), tasked with overseeing the reconstruction of the temple (Ezra 5:3).
H6347.origine: The Aramaic word pechah comes from the same root as the Hebrew pachah (פַּחָה), which literally means "one who administers" or "one who governs." This root expresses the idea of prescribing, ordering, directing. The word is used in the Persian and Babylonian empires to designate high-ranking officials responsible for regions or provinces.
H6347.emploi: The term appears ten times in the Bible, almost entirely in the books of Ezra and Daniel, during the period when the Jews live under Persian or Babylonian domination. In Ezra, the governors are Persians like Tattenai and Shethar-Bozenai, who supervise the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem and report to King Darius (Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6, 6:13). In Daniel, the term also appears to designate high officials of the kingdom (Daniel 3:2). These governors have administrative and judicial authority, but they remain subject to royal power.
H6347.portee: The word governor reminds the reader that, even during exile and reconstruction, God governs political events. The Persian governors, despite their apparent power, ultimately become instruments of divine will: Darius eventually authorizes and supports the reconstruction of the temple (Ezra 6:6-7). This shows that the Lord directs the hearts of kings and that His promise of restoration is fulfilled despite obstacles.

sens: To act impulsively, without restraint or reflection
To lack seriousness or respect in one's behavior
To be turbulent, careless of the consequences
H6348.detail:
1. This verb describes a person who acts without restraint, driven by the impulse of the moment. In Judges 9:4, Abimelech recruits "turbulent" men — scoundrels who are reckless and unscrupulous — to follow him in his quest for power. It is the image of someone who is not held back by anything, who rushes in without thinking.
2. The word also suggests a guilty lightness, a lack of respect for what should be taken seriously. In Zephaniah 3:4, the prophets of Jerusalem are described as "rash," meaning they speak without reverence, unfaithful to their sacred mission. It is the attitude of one who treats lightly what demands respect.
H6348.origine: This root evokes the image of something that bubbles or stirs without control — like light and turbulent foam on the surface of water. The verb thus naturally describes a person or action devoid of stability and gravity.
H6348.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Judges 9:4, it qualifies the henchmen that Abimelech buys to overthrow the city of Shechem — men without morals, ready to do anything for money. In Zephaniah 3:4, it describes the false prophets of Jerusalem, who proclaim light and disrespectful words towards God. In both cases, it is a serious moral flaw: the absence of restraint and fear.
H6348.portee: This word warns us against impulsiveness and lack of reflection. It calls us to cultivate restraint, respect, and the fear of God, rather than acting on a whim. It is an invitation to examine our motives and actions before embarking on an endeavor.

sens: impulsive character, without restraint
lack of self-control
inconstancy, frivolity in behavior
H6349.detail:
1. Impetuosity refers to an impulsive temperament that acts without thinking and without control — like water flowing violently, unable to be contained. In Genesis 49:4, Jacob reproaches Reuben for his 'impetuous' character: he acted without restraint, in a passionate surge that led him to commit a serious and shameful act.
2. It also signifies a lack of moral stability, a frivolity that prevents one from attaining maturity and responsibility. An impetuous person cannot maintain a position of power or dignity, as they do not control their impulses.
H6349.origine: The Hebrew word פַּחַז (pachaz) originally evokes the image of something light and unstable, almost foamy. The context of Genesis 49:4 establishes a contrast: while water flows forcefully, it cannot retain shape or authority. The root expresses the idea of moral lightness and lack of solid foundation.
H6349.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 49:4, in Jacob's final blessing on his sons. Jacob uses it to characterize Reuben, his firstborn son, who should have enjoyed the birthright and the honor it confers. But instead, Reuben committed a serious transgression (he dishonored his father's bed), revealing a fundamental inability to control his passions. Through this reproach, Jacob makes it clear that Reuben will not receive preeminence: his impetuosity — his lack of wisdom and restraint — disqualifies him.
H6349.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the link between character and destiny. One who acts without self-control, driven by impulses, loses not only the esteem of others but also the blessings and responsibilities that could have been theirs. It is a call to cultivate self-control and reflection before acting.

sens: lightness of mind, lack of reflection
reckless boldness, irresponsible daring
extravagance, excess without restraint
frivolity, lack of seriousness
H6350.detail:
1. Temerity is primarily a lightness of mind: it is acting without thinking, without weighing the consequences, as if the weight of things does not affect us. It is a form of unconsciousness.
2. It manifests as reckless boldness: one dares to do or say things without true fear, but without wisdom either. In Jeremiah 23:32, the false prophets speak with this reckless audacity, asserting lies without fearing God's judgment.
3. Temerity produces extravagance: one exceeds reasonable limits, wastes, abuses. The false prophets mislead the people with their lies precisely because they speak with this irresponsibility.
4. Finally, it is a frivolity, a lack of seriousness in the face of grave matters. When one prophesies without God having spoken (Jeremiah 23:32), one treats the word of the Lord with a guilty lightness.
H6350.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of lightness, lack of weight or substance. It designates one who is 'light' in judgment, who lacks depth. Temerity is the opposite of wisdom and the fear of the Lord: it is acting as if the world has no moral order, as if God does not exist.
H6350.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 23:32. The prophet Jeremiah denounces the false prophets who lie to the people and mislead them. God says He will take action against those who 'tell false dreams' and who 'lead my people astray with their lies and their temerity.' Here, the temerity of the false prophets is their unfounded confidence, their audacity to speak without having received a mission from God. It is a severe judgment: God neither sent nor commanded them, and their words benefit the people nothing.
H6350.portee: The temerity denounced here invites the believer to distinguish true boldness (that of faith in God) from false boldness (that which ignores God and His commandments). It warns us against seductive but empty words that promise without foundation. For the Christian, it is a call to seriousness, wisdom, and respect for the word of God: not to act lightly in spiritual matters.

sens: to put someone in chains, to imprison them
to capture, to trap, to hold someone in one's power
H6351.detail:
1. To chain literally means to put chains on someone, to immobilize them and deprive them of freedom. In Isaiah 42:22, God describes an unhappy people: 'They are all chained in caves, plunged into dungeons,' an image of brutal and humiliating captivity where men are bound and confined.
2. More broadly, the word expresses the idea of being trapped or subjected: to chain someone is to reduce them to helplessness, to submit them to a domination from which they cannot escape. It is the condition of a victim stripped and without help.
H6351.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּחַח (pachach) comes from a root that evokes the action of seizing, capturing, or clamping down. The form used here (Hiphil) reinforces the meaning: it shifts the action from a passive state to an active action imposed by an agent — 'to make someone be chained,' in other words, 'to put in chains.' This word belongs to the biblical vocabulary of captivity and servitude.
H6351.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 42:22. God denounces the misery of a stripped, plundered, imprisoned people — likely Israel in exile or oppressed. The prophet uses it to paint a picture of extreme distress: chained in caves, deprived of freedom and help. It is a rare and expressive word, reserved for this moment of divine indignation in the face of injustice.
H6351.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the slavery of sin and evil is a serious spiritual reality. Just as a chained people cannot free themselves, the human heart captive to evil needs a deliverance that comes from God. It is a call to recognize one's distress and to hope for a deliverer.

sens: a piece of wood or combustible material partially burned, glowing and giving off heat
glowing ember from a hearth or forge
image of a quarrel or anger that ignites
H6352.detail:
1. Coal is wood that has begun to burn and glows intensely, giving off lasting heat without bright flames. This is what the blacksmith uses to work metal: in Isaiah 44:12, the blacksmith 'works with coal' to heat his iron and shape it with a hammer.
2. More broadly, it refers to the ember or hot material that remains ardent long after the initial combustion. In Isaiah 54:16, God speaks of one 'who blows the coal into the fire,' meaning the bellows operator who stokes the coals to maintain intense heat.
3. The Bible also uses this word to evoke a heated quarrel: in Proverbs 26:21, 'coal produces a blaze,' just as a quarrelsome person 'kindles a dispute.' Coal becomes the image of what ignites and spreads: a harsh word can ignite a conflict, just as a glowing coal rekindles a fire.
H6352.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּחָם (pecham) designates charcoal or ember. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of roasting or glowing. The word refers to the very concrete image of the hearth, the forge, and ancient cooking, where coal was the primary source of heat and energy for metalworking and cooking.
H6352.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with work or conflict. In Isaiah, it refers to the coal of the forge: it is the fuel that the blacksmith uses to heat and transform metal into tools or weapons (Isaiah 44:12 and 54:16). In Proverbs, the word shifts to a more figurative sense: coal illustrates the flammable nature of quarrels, how a dispute can ignite and spread like fire (Proverbs 26:21). This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how the Bible draws on everyday images to speak of spiritual or moral realities.
H6352.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on two levels. First, on the power of transformation: coal, in the hands of the blacksmith, becomes a tool of creation. Second, on the danger of angry words: just as a coal can rekindle a fire, a harsh word can ignite a conflict and destroy relationships. It is a call to vigilance and self-control.

sens: Worker who shapes clay to make vases, containers, and other ceramic objects
One who possesses the skill and authority to create and form matter
Metaphorically, one who shapes, creates, or governs according to their will
H6353.detail:
1. The potter is the artisan who works with wet clay to create useful or decorative containers and objects. It is an ancient and respected trade in the biblical world. In Daniel 2:41, Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream a statue whose feet are made of a mixture of potter's clay and iron: the potter's clay here refers to the fragile ceramic of the potter, fragile compared to iron.
2. By extension, the potter represents one who has creative power and authority over their material: they shape it at will, transforming it according to their intention. This is why biblical prophets and sages use the image of the potter to speak of God who creates, forms the people, and governs nations according to His sovereign will.
H6353.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּחָר (pechar) literally means "one who shapes clay" or "pottery maker." It comes from the context of the artisanal work of the ancient Near East, where pottery was a vital industry for making containers, amphorae, and dishes. The word is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible, but the image of the potter is often used to represent the Creator God who shapes His people as one shapes clay.
H6353.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 2:41, in the interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic dream. In this context, "potter's clay" refers to fragile and easily breakable ceramic, contrasting with the solidity of iron. The term evokes both an ordinary and concrete trade, and implicitly refers to the biblical imagery of the potter as creator and shaper, a theme that is extensively developed elsewhere in the prophets, particularly in Jeremiah.
H6353.portee: The image of the potter reminds the reader that God is the sovereign creator who shapes nations and peoples according to His plan. It invites recognition of our fragility and dependence on the One who created us, while emphasizing that our existence has meaning and direction given by the Creator. It is an invitation to confident submission to divine will.

sens: Hole dug in the ground or natural cavity in the earth
Trap or danger where one falls and from which escape is not easy
Place of death or annihilation
H6354.detail:
1. A pit is primarily a hole dug in the ground or a natural cavity: it is a deep hollow into which one can fall or hide. Absalom is thrown into a great pit in the middle of the forest (2 Samuel 18:17), and David must hide in some pit to escape his pursuers (2 Samuel 17:9).
2. The pit becomes an image of the trap: it symbolizes a danger from which one cannot escape. Isaiah lists the three perils threatening the land: "terror, the pit, and the net" (Isaiah 24:17). One who flees from one falls into another, showing how misfortune surrounds us on all sides (Isaiah 24:18).
3. In figurative language, the pit represents death or destruction: it is an abyss from which no one returns. This meaning appears in the lamentations of the prophet who cries that terror, the pit, and the net threaten him (Lamentations 3:47).
H6354.origine: The Hebrew word פַּחַת comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or making a hole. The same word is used to designate both a natural cave (as in Jeremiah 48:28, where doves nest on the slopes of the caves) and a pit dug by man. It is a concrete word that first describes a physical reality of the terrain, before becoming a powerful image of danger and death.
H6354.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets and the history of the kings. In 2 Samuel, it refers to actual pits where one hides or where the dead are thrown (Absalom thrown into a pit). In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations), it takes on a figurative sense: the pit becomes a symbol of inevitable misfortune and death. Isaiah 24:17-18 couples it with "terror" and "the net" to express how the three calamities surround humans. In Jeremiah 48:43-44, the same enumeration applies to Moab. This passage shows how a concrete word gradually becomes a prophetic cry.
H6354.portee: The pit reminds us that sin and misfortune surround humanity: there is no escape by one's own strength. It is an image that urges recognition of our dependence on God and His salvation. But it also invites vigilance: fleeing sin means not falling into the trap that God keeps us from crossing.

sens: Man who lived during the time of the exile and the return of Israel
Ancestor of one or two families of Israel who returned from captivity in Babylon
Leader of the people involved in the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the community life of the return
H6355G.detail: 1. Pachath-Moab is a man whose name appears in the lists of the people returning from Babylonian exile during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. His name, which literally means "pit of Moab," may reveal an origin linked to the region of Moab, or a mixed ancestry. 2. He is best known as the ancestor of a large family: in Ezra 2:6 and Nehemiah 7:11, more than two thousand eight hundred men returned from captivity among his descendants, making it one of the most important families of the return. 3. Beyond this genealogical role, Pachath-Moab is mentioned as a figure of responsibility in the restored community: in Ezra 10:30, men of his descent are involved in important decisions of the people, notably the dismissal of foreign wives. He thus represents one of the pillar families of Judah restored after the exile.
H6355G.origine: The name Pachath-Moab literally means "pit of Moab." Its precise meaning remains subject to debate: it may designate an ancestor who had a connection with the historical region of Moab (east of Jordan), or mark a genealogical particularity. In any case, this name remains associated with one of the great families of the return from exile, and it is known only through these biblical lists.
H6355G.emploi: Pachath-Moab appears four times in the Bible, always in the context of the return from Babylonian exile, around the fifth century B.C. In Ezra 2:6, he is the father of Joshua and Joab, whose descendants (more than 2,812 people) return from captivity; the same list, with a slightly different number, appears in Nehemiah 7:11. In Ezra 8:4, a leader bearing his name (or from his descent) brings two hundred men from his family. Finally, in Ezra 10:30, several men of his descent actively participate in the reorganization of the people and their commitments to God. These uses show that Pachath-Moab embodies one of the founding families of post-exilic Judah.

sens: man living during the time of exile and return
leader among the Israelites who returned from captivity
H6355H.detail: Pahath-Moab is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites return from exile in Babylon. His name literally means "pit of Moab" or "well of Moab," likely a nickname or title rather than a birth name. He is presented as an important leader of the people: his son Hasshub participates in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:11), which shows the influence and authority of his family.
H6355H.origine: The name Pahath-Moab is composed of two Hebrew parts: "pahath" (pit, well) and "Moab" (the neighboring country of Israel, east of the Dead Sea). This name could allude to a region, a function, or a characteristic associated with Moab, although its exact historical meaning is not clarified in the available biblical texts. It is a patronymic name, a family lineage carries this name in post-exilic Israel.
H6355H.emploi: Pahath-Moab is named only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:11, in the context of the return from exile in Babylon and the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem. His son Hasshub is mentioned as one of the workers participating in this great restoration. He is also counted among the leaders of the people and the signers of the renewal of the covenant with God. This unique mention suggests that he was a prominent figure among those who led the Israelite community during this decisive turning point in Israel's history.
H6355H.portee: Pahath-Moab represents one of those leaders whose discreet yet concrete action was decisive in the survival and restoration of God's people after the exile. His commitment to rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem and renewing the covenant with the Lord shows that restoration did not depend on a single charismatic figure, but on the faithfulness of many servants. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that God uses unknown faithful individuals to accomplish His purposes.

sens: Leader of the people returned from exile who signed the covenant with Nehemiah
H6355I.detail: Pachath-Moab (whose name literally means "pit of Moab") is a leader of the people mentioned during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He appears in the list of leaders who solemnly committed to the covenant with Nehemiah after the reconstruction of the city walls. His name may also refer to the family or clan he represented among the exiles returned from Babylon.
H6355I.origine: The name Pachath-Moab is composed of two Hebrew elements: "pachath" meaning "pit" or "well," and "Moab" is the name of a neighboring people of Israel located east of the Jordan. The origin and exact meaning of this name remain enigmatic; it may be a nickname or a geographical feature. The name appears in the genealogies of those who returned from captivity.
H6355I.emploi: Pachath-Moab is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:14, among the leaders of the people who publicly acknowledged the God of Israel and committed to a solemn covenant. His name appears in an official list alongside other leaders such as Pahath-Moab and Elam. This man or leader evidently represented an important family among the repatriated from Babylon, significant enough to be among the signers of this crucial pact.

sens: Hole or hollow that forms
Progressive destruction of a material
Cavity caused by leprosy in a garment
H6356.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a hole or hollow that forms in a surface, through erosion or gradual wear — the image of something sinking, emptying from within.
2. It is a destruction that advances little by little: a material erodes, consumes, hollows out.
3. In the context of Leviticus 13:55, the word describes the visible sign of leprosy on a garment — a cavity or a rotted area that shows the disease has attacked the fabric deeply. It is not just a stain, but a real damage to the material.
H6356.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of digging, piercing, or eroding. The root suggests a progressive action, almost a gnawing: the image is that of leprosy which does not destroy at once, but slowly erodes the garment from within.
H6356.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 13:55, in the detailed description of the laws concerning leprosy. The priests of Israel had to examine a garment suspected of leprosy to check if the disease had dug a hole or cavity in the fabric. This perforation confirmed that the garment was unclean and had to be burned. The context is clearly that of ritual purity and medical-ritual diagnosis among the people of God.
H6356.portee: This word reminds us that biblical leprosy is a disease that destroys and spreads: it does not leave intact, it creates visible damage. For the believer, it is an image of how sin or impurity progresses — not in a stroke, but by gnawing, hollowing out, leaving marks. The diagnosis requires vigilance: one must know how to recognize when evil has truly penetrated and really damaged.

sens: Yellow or yellow-green precious stone, very hard and shiny
In the high priest's garment, one of the stones of the breastplate symbolizing the twelve tribes
Symbol of divine beauty and wealth
H6357.detail:
1. Topaz is a precious stone sought after for its hardness and brilliance. It can be yellow or yellow-green, and the Ancients considered it one of the most beautiful stones. In Job 28:19, it is named alongside pure gold to assess the incomparable value of divine Wisdom: "The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, Nor can it be valued in pure gold."
2. God commanded the high priest of Israel to set a topaz in the breastplate (Exodus 28:17 and 39:10), the fourth stone of the first row, symbolizing one of the tribes: this use shows that it was both precious and easily identifiable for the artisans of the tabernacle.
3. Ezekiel 28:13 describes the king of Tyre adorned with all kinds of precious stones including topaz: this image evokes the created splendor that God grants, but also the pride that corrupts beauty.
H6357.origine: The Hebrew word פִּטְדָה may come from a root meaning "to shine" or "to glow." The name simply reflects the direct observation of a very common natural stone in Egypt and Ethiopia. Ethiopian topaz was particularly famous in the ancient world for its exceptional quality.
H6357.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate this precious stone. Three occurrences concern the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28 and 39), where it is part of the twelve stones representing the tribes of Israel. One occurrence in Job mentions it to show the immeasurable value of divine Wisdom compared to all earthly riches. A final appearance in Ezekiel's vision places it among the ornaments of the king of Tyre, symbols of his beauty before the fall. Topaz is always listed with other precious stones, never isolated, which emphasizes that it belongs to the order of authentic treasures.
H6357.portee: Topaz reminds the believer that God loves true and lasting beauty, not illusion. It invites the pursuit of divine Wisdom rather than earthly riches (Job 28), and to recognize that all beauty comes from the Creator. Finally, it warns that beauty without God becomes destructive pride (Ezekiel 28).

sens: Tool used to strike and shape metal or stone
Image of divine power that breaks and transforms
Symbol of destructive force or domination
H6360.detail:
1. The hammer is the tool of the blacksmith and the sculptor: in Isaiah 41:7, the one who smooths with the hammer encourages the founder who works on the idol. It is a manual work instrument, intended to strike and shape hard materials (metal, stone, rock).
2. The word of God is compared to a hammer that breaks the rock (Jeremiah 23:29). This image evokes a transformative power: just as the hammer strikes and shatters inert stone, the divine word strikes the heart and breaks resistance, producing an irresistible and profound effect.
3. In Jeremiah 50:23, Babylon itself is called "the hammer of all the earth," designating its dominating strength and power to subdue nations. When this hammer is broken, it signifies the collapse of a conquering empire; the word takes on a political and symbolic significance.
H6360.origine: The Hebrew word is formed from a root that denotes the action of striking and shaping. It refers to the concrete image of the blacksmith's and carpenter's working tool, an instrument that naturally appears in the building trades and craftsmanship of the Old Testament. The Bible uses this word to transition from the material object to spiritual or political realities: the hammer becomes a symbol of active power.
H6360.emploi: The word hammer appears three times in the Bible. In Isaiah 41:7, it refers to the tool of the sculptor who shapes idols. In Jeremiah 23:29, it is the image used by the prophet to describe the effect of the divine word: it breaks, it transforms, it imposes its will just as a hammer imposes its shape on matter. In Jeremiah 50:23, Babylon, "the hammer of all the earth," loses its strength and collapses: the word then expresses the international dominance of a power that is falling. Each time, the hammer embodies an active power that strikes, breaks, transforms, or subdues.
H6360.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the power of the word of God: it is not soft or harmless; it acts with force and produces irreversible results, like a hammer striking the rock. It also teaches that all human domination, even the most formidable (Babylon), ultimately collapses: only the word of God remains, breaking and transforming.

sens: Garment worn on the body, under a coat or outer garment
H6361.detail: 1. An outer or mid-season garment, worn directly on the skin or over a light shirt, resembling a kind of tunic or sleeveless dress. In the passage from Daniel, the three young men are thrown into the furnace wearing their tunics along with other clothing items. It is a common garment in the ancient Near East, practical for the climate and daily activities.
H6361.origine: The Hebrew word פְּטַשׁ (pattish) designates an element of clothing; its exact root and etymology remain uncertain, but it belongs to the vocabulary of garments specific to the Babylonian context of Daniel. The word is rare in the Hebrew Bible.
H6361.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:21, during the account of the three young men refusing to worship the statue of Nebuchadnezzar. The mention of the tunic is part of the description of what they were wearing at the time of their condemnation to the furnace, emphasizing that even their ordinary clothing would not be consumed by the miraculous fire. It is a realistic and vivid detail of the narrative that reinforces the extraordinary nature of their deliverance.
H6361.portee: This passage reminds us that God protects those who remain faithful to His commandments, even in the midst of the most extreme persecutions. The detail of the intact clothing shows that nothing can truly harm those who trust in God.

sens: to flee, to evade a danger or threat
to remove, to distance oneself from something approaching
to open up, to bloom (referring to a flower or decoration)
to be freed from an obligation, exemption from a duty
H6362.detail:
1. To flee or save oneself from peril: it is to leave a place quickly to avoid being harmed. When David played before Saul, the king, seized with madness, threw his spear at him. David "turned away from him" and escaped to survive (1 Samuel 19:10).
2. To push away or repel something coming towards oneself: it is to make a movement to avoid it. David also had to evade the threat.
3. To bloom, like a flower opening: this very different meaning appears in descriptions of the Temple, where the cedar bore carvings of "blooming flowers" (1 Kings 6:18, 6:29), ornamental and delicate, opened in full beauty.
