4. To be freed, liberated from a burden or obligation: it is not being subject to a service. The Levitical singers, residing in the Temple chambers, were "exempt" from other duties because they sang day and night in the service of God (1 Chronicles 9:33).
H6362.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּטַר comes from a root that suggests the idea of separation and liberation. The basic image is that of opening, liberating, clearing. The root appears in the name פִּטְרַת, the birthright or portion received by the firstborn by being "separated" from the other sons. In biblical Hebrew, this verb oscillates between the concrete idea of moving away or turning aside and that of liberating or exempting from a burden.
H6362.emploi: This verb appears about nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and descriptions of the Temple. In action narratives (1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles), it expresses the act of escaping or evading an immediate danger. In the architectural descriptions of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6), it designates the blooming of sculpted flowers, a flourishing ornamentation. Finally, in a context of religious service (1 Chronicles 9:33), it means being exempted from other tasks. The meaning thus varies: from the concrete and dramatic (fleeing) to the decorative and administrative (exempting).
H6362.portee: This word reminds us that fleeing from peril is not cowardice when it is wisdom: David escapes from Saul because God protects him and intends him for a future reign. It also invites us to contemplate the created beauty — the blooming flowers of the Temple symbolize the splendor and life that God brings to all things. Finally, the exemption of the singers shows that certain tasks — here worship — are so precious that they free one from all other burdens.

sens: The first child born of a mother, particularly the eldest son
The male animal born first in a litter or flock
That which comes out or appears first, which opens the way
One who has the right of primogeniture and special blessing
H6363A.detail:
1. The firstborn is the child who comes into the world first from a mother. In the Bible, this is primarily a physical fact: the one who "opens the womb" (Exodus 13:2). This status is not ordinary: it confers special rights and a place of honor in the family.

2. Similarly, the firstborn of livestock is the male that is born first in a flock. Exodus 13:12 and 34:19 show that these animals belong to God and must be consecrated or redeemed by a lamb (Exodus 13:13).

3. The imagery of the word is that of what "separates" or "opens": the firstborn is the one who first crosses the threshold of life, who initiates the lineage. This is the original meaning of the Hebrew root, expressing the idea of breakthrough or opening.

4. Spiritually and legally, the firstborn benefits from a special blessing and consecration to God. Exodus 13:15 links this reality to the memory of the tenth plague of Egypt, where God struck all the firstborn of the Egyptians: henceforth, every firstborn of Israel belongs to the Lord and must be redeemed or offered as a sacrifice.
H6363A.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּטֶר (péter) comes from a root that literally means "to open" or "to pierce." The firstborn is the one who "opens" the maternal womb. This link to opening explains why the same root can also mean that which "flows" or spills out (hence the secondary meaning of "source" or "flow"). The notion of separation (the newborn separating from its mother) reinforces this image of rupture or crossing a boundary.
H6363A.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Bible, primarily in the consecration code of Exodus 13 and 34, which frames the Exodus from Egypt. Exodus 13:2, 13:12, and 34:19 stipulate that every firstborn belongs to the Lord. Exodus 13:13 and 34:20 prescribe the redemption of the firstborn of the donkey by a lamb, and of the firstborn of the sons by a redemption (monetary or sacrificial). Exodus 13:15 ties this commandment to the tenth plague, where the Lord struck the firstborns of Egypt. Passages in Numbers (3:12, 18:15) and Ezekiel (20:26) use the term in contexts of consecration or judgment, always in connection with a right or belonging to God.
H6363A.portee: The firstborn reveals that God claims life itself and the firstborn, the beginning. This law shows the chosen people that they own nothing of their own: everything comes from God and is consecrated to Him. Redeeming the firstborn is to acknowledge that life is a gift and that we are redeemed. This practice anchors the Exodus in memory: each generation remembers that God spared the firstborns of Israel and struck those of Egypt, a deliverance that must never be forgotten.

sens: The eldest son of a family, the one who is born first
In a ritual or legal sense: one who has special rights in inheritance and worship
That which opens or separates, which comes first from the womb of its mother
H6363B.detail:
1. The firstborn is the eldest son, the first child born in a family. It is a special status that marks his entire life and that of his descendants.
2. In the Bible, the firstborn does not only receive an honorary status: he inherits a double portion of the father's goods and plays a special role in family and national worship. In Numbers 8:16, God says that He has taken the Levites "in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel," which shows that the firstborns of Israel originally belonged to God in a special way.
3. The word literally designates that which "opens" or "separates": the child who first crosses the threshold of life by leaving the mother's womb. It is the physical act before any legal privilege.
H6363B.origine: The Hebrew word pit.rah comes from the root ptr (פ-ט-ר) which literally means "to open" or "to separate." The firstborn "opens" or "separates" the womb by being the first to be born. This same root generates several words in the family: pèter (פֶּטֶר), which is another form of "firstborn." The imagery is very concrete: it is the child who breaks or crosses first, who comes first.
H6363B.emploi: This word is rare in the Bible: it appears only once in Numbers 8:16, where God commands that the Levites be set apart for the service of the Tabernacle "in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel." This reveals a fundamental principle: originally, all the firstborns of Israel belonged to God by a special link, due to their status as firstborns. After the ten plagues of Egypt and the sacrifice of the Passover, God "consecrated" this relationship by designating the Levites to replace them in this role of service to God.
H6363B.portee: The firstborn symbolizes one who belongs entirely to God and is set apart for His service. For the Christian, this reminds us that our life is also bought and consecrated to God; we are "redeemed" just as the firstborns of Egypt were by the blood of the Passover lamb. The status of firstborn also invites a special responsibility: one who receives more must serve more.

sens: City of ancient Egypt
Ancient city of Lower Egypt
H6364.detail: 1. Pi-Béseth is a city of ancient Egypt, located in Lower Egypt on the west bank of the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, about 65 kilometers from Memphis. The name means "mouth of the loathing" or "dwelling of Bastet," the Egyptian goddess with a cat's head worshiped in this region. 2. In the prophecy of Ezekiel against Egypt, Pi-Béseth is among the Egyptian cities that will suffer divine judgment: "The young men of On and Pi-Béseth will fall by the sword, and these cities will go into captivity" (Ezekiel 30:17). This mention emphasizes that even the important urban centers of Egypt will not be spared by God's judgment.
H6364.origine: The name "Pi-Béseth" is an Egyptian name that literally means "house of Bastet" or "mouth of the goddess Bastet." In ancient geography, it is often identified with Bubastis, an important sanctuary dedicated to the feline goddess Bastet. This site was a major religious and commercial center of ancient Lower Egypt.
H6364.emploi: Pi-Béseth appears only once in the Bible, in the prophecy of Ezekiel directed against Egypt (Ezekiel 30:17). It is mentioned alongside other famous Egyptian cities like On (Heliopolis) in a context of divine judgment upon the Egyptian nation. Its inclusion in this list of prophetic judgments underscores the importance and notoriety of this city among the major centers of ancient Egypt.

sens: Ruin, destruction, collapse
State of one who is struck by fate, who suffers
Sudden calamity that befalls someone
Dreaded disastrous event
H6365.detail:
1. Misfortune is primarily a concrete ruin, a reversal of fortune: it is what happens to one whose "foot slips" (Job 12:5), whose life collapses. The word evokes a fall, a catastrophe that destroys.
2. It is also the state of suffering and distress of one who undergoes this reversal: one who is "in misfortune" (Job 30:24) implores help, hands outstretched, for they are in peril.
3. Misfortune can also be a calamity that suddenly arises: a ruin that "will arise" without warning (Proverbs 24:22), striking its targets by surprise.
4. Finally, it is what is dreaded and can be wickedly rejoiced over: one who boasts of the "misfortune" of their enemy (Job 31:29) savors their destruction with malicious joy.
H6365.origine: The word belongs to the family of Hebrew that evokes the idea of tipping over, falling, collapsing. It expresses a sudden rupture of balance, the transition from good to evil, from stability to ruin. This image of fall or collapse structures the entire meaning of the word in the Bible.
H6365.emploi: This word appears four times in biblical Hebrew, only in the wisdom books (Job and Proverbs). Job uses it to describe the reversal of fortune that the righteous suffer and that the fortunate despise (12:5), or the extreme distress of one who perishes and pleads (30:24, 31:29). In Proverbs 24:22, misfortune is a ruin that suddenly befalls those who are rebellious to authority. The word always depicts a catastrophic, brutal event that radically changes a person's destiny.
H6365.portee: This word challenges the reader regarding their attitude toward the misfortune of others. The Bible warns against the cruel satisfaction of seeing an enemy perish (Job 31:29): one who rejoices in another's misfortune commits a sin. It also invites compassion toward those who suffer, for misfortune can strike anyone, anytime, and those who fall need help, not contempt.

sens: Sharp edge of a blade or a cutting weapon
Cutting side of a weapon (sword, knife)
H6366.detail:
1. The edge is the sharpened side of a blade that allows for cutting. It is the fine, sharp ridge of the metal. Ehud, a leader of Israel, carries a double-edged sword: this means it cuts on both sides, like a double blade (Judges 3:16).

2. By extension, the edge refers to the cutting side of a weapon intended for combat or work. It is the active part, the one that wounds or slices.
H6366.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of side, face, that which looks forward. In Hebrew, פֵּה (peh) primarily means "mouth," but the root can also express the idea of "opening" or "side." Here, פֵּיָה refers to the edge that opens, that points toward the target: the edge is what faces the opponent. The word has a characteristic feminine form.
H6366.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Judges 3:16, where it describes Ehud's sword. This double-edged sword is a detail of the narrative that emphasizes the danger of the weapon and Ehud's premeditation, who carries this secret weapon to accomplish his mission against Eglon, king of Moab. The technical term "double-edged" reinforces the idea of a formidable and well-thought-out weapon.
H6366.portee: This word reminds us that the weapons of physical combat can be deadly. It prepares the reader to understand that violence, even justified by the liberation of Israel, requires courage and cunning. It is also an opportunity to meditate on the biblical image of the Word of God, often compared to a double-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12), which pierces the heart with formidable precision.

sens: Place in Egypt where the Israelites camp before crossing the Red Sea
Location near the sea, between Migdol and Baal-Zephon
Area where Pharaoh's army catches up with the Israelites
H6367.detail:
1. Pi-Hahiroth is a geographical site in Egypt, the penultimate campsite of the Israelites after their departure from Goshen (Exodus 14:2). The name literally means "mouth of the reeds" or "where reeds grow," suggesting a marshy or coastal region. It is here, near the sea, that God will perform the miracle of the crossing (Exodus 14:9).
2. The place is precisely located between two landmarks: Migdol to the west and Baal-Zephon to the east, directly at the edge of the sea (Exodus 14:2). This framed location shows that it is a strategic passage point, a bottleneck where the Israelites appear to be trapped.
3. It is at Pi-Hahiroth that Pharaoh's army joins the people of Israel while they are camping (Exodus 14:9). This place thus becomes the theater of the final conflict between Pharaoh and the God of Israel, just before the sea opens.
H6367.origine: The Hebrew name פִּי הַחִירֹת (pi ha-chirot) is composed of פִּי (pi, "mouth," "mouthpiece") and חִירֹת (chirot, "reeds"). This descriptive name reflects the local geography: a coastal or deltaic area planted with aquatic vegetation, typical of ancient northeastern Egypt. The name refers to the physical reality of the landscape rather than a legendary event.
H6367.emploi: Pi-Hahiroth appears four times in the Bible, all in the context of the Exodus. Exodus 14 mentions this place twice: first as the site where God commands the Israelites to camp (14:2), then as the place where Pharaoh catches up with them with his army (14:9). Numbers 33 mentions it twice in the itinerary account of the camps: Numbers 33:7 indicates that the Israelites turn toward Pi-Hahiroth after Etham, and Numbers 33:8 marks their departure from this same place to cross the sea. The name appears only in these two historical books and remains attached to this foundational episode.
H6367.portee: Pi-Hahiroth symbolizes the critical moment when God traps the people between the sea and the enemy army, creating the conditions for the miracle. This place reminds us that divine deliverance often arises in seemingly impossible situations: it is there, in a humanly impossible circumstance, that the power of God fully manifests. The name of the place invites the believer to see in the most distressing circumstances the space where God accomplishes His salvation.

sens: Fine black dust resulting from the burning of coal or wood
Pulverulent residue left after intense fire
Symbol of divine judgment or destruction
H6368.detail:
1. Furnace ash is the fine black dust that remains when coal or wood is burned at very high temperatures. It is a very fine powder, easily dispersed by the wind. In Exodus 9:8, Moses and Aaron fill their hands with this ash from a furnace.
2. More broadly, it is the pulverulent and gray residue that remains after an intense fire. This dust can be thrown into the air and spread easily, as Moses does by casting it "toward the sky" (Exodus 9:10).
3. Biblically, furnace ash is not just an ordinary material: it is an instrument of God's judgment. When Moses throws it, it turns into a plague causing sores on men and animals (Exodus 9:10), showing that God can transform a simple material into punishment.
H6368.origine: The Hebrew word piach literally means fine dust or soot produced by combustion. It evokes the image of a black and light powder, easily dispersed. The biblical context often associates ash with furnaces, symbolizing destruction and divine judgment.
H6368.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:8 and 9:10). In these two verses, the furnace ash is taken by Moses and Aaron, then thrown by Moses before Pharaoh. This divine action transforms ordinary ash into a miraculous plague: it produces sores and pustules on the Egyptians and their animals. The word always designates this specific furnace ash, never the ordinary ash of a hearth, emphasizing its extraordinary and miraculous nature.
H6368.portee: This furnace ash reminds the reader that God completely masters the elements of creation and can use them to execute His judgment. It also illustrates Pharaoh's powerlessness in the face of divine power: even a simple powder becomes, in Moses' hands, an invincible instrument of punishment. For the believer, it is a sign that God does not need any spectacular instrument to manifest His authority; His command is sufficient.

sens: Philistine military chief during the time of the Patriarchs
Trusted officer of King Abimelech
H6369.detail: Picol is a high-ranking military chief in the service of King Abimelech of Gerar (a coastal region of the Philistines). He accompanies the king during important negotiations with Abraham and Isaac, which shows his high status. He is mentioned three times in Genesis: first in Genesis 21:22 when Abimelech and he come to make a covenant with Abraham, then in Genesis 21:32 when they rise to return to the land of the Philistines after sealing the agreement at Beersheba, and finally in Genesis 26:26 when Abimelech returns, accompanied by Picol, to deal with Isaac, Abraham's son.
H6369.origine: The name Picol means "strong" or "mighty" in Hebrew. It is a typical Semitic name of ancient Philistine kings and chiefs. Its systematic inclusion alongside King Abimelech in the accounts of the Patriarchs suggests that he was a prominent historical figure, likely the commander-in-chief of the armies of the land.
H6369.emploi: Picol appears three times in the book of Genesis, always alongside the Philistine king Abimelech. In the accounts of Abraham (Genesis 21:22 and 21:32), he represents the military power of Gerar and participates in the conclusion of a peace covenant. A generation later (Genesis 26:26), the same name reappears with Abimelech alongside Isaac, indicating either the continuity of a Philistine dynasty or a transmission of the name in the succession of military leaders. His role remains constant: that of an influential man alongside the king, capable of negotiating with the Patriarchs.
H6369.portee: Picol embodies the political and military authority of non-Israelite powers in the ancient Near East. His presence in the accounts of the Patriarchs shows that God placed His servants at the heart of contexts of peace and alliance with neighboring peoples. The appearance of the same name alongside Abimelech invites reflection on the continuity of power structures and how God guided the affairs of nations in the design of protecting His people.

sens: woman united to a man outside of official marriage
wife of lower rank in a polygamous context
woman maintained by a man without recognized wife status
H6370.detail:
1. A concubine is a woman who lives with a man without being his wife in the full sense of the law and custom. Unlike a wife, she does not have the same social status or rights. In Genesis 22:24, Reumah is referred to as Abraham's "concubine": she bears his children but holds a distinct rank from Sarah.

2. In the marital life of kings and powerful men, the concubine is a woman of the household, often taken from captives or women of lower status, who shares the master's life but is not his primary wife. King David had many concubines (2 Samuel 5:13), as did Solomon (1 Kings 11:3).

3. The story of the Levite and his concubine (Judges 19) shows the vulnerability of this woman: although she lives with him, she may be exposed to dangers and does not have the protection that a wife would have. Her lack of official marital status makes her position fragile in society.
H6370.origine: The Hebrew word פִּלֶגֶשׁ (piléguèsh) appears in the ancient Near East with this specific meaning. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it designates a well-established social reality in antiquity: a woman attached to a man, living under his roof, but without the legal and social status of a wife. It is a technical term of family law of the time.
H6370.emploi: The word appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical accounts of judges and kings. Abraham has a concubine (Genesis 25:6), as do Caleb and other high-ranking men. Kings have several: David and Solomon possess harems of concubines listed to show their power. The account of Judges 19-20 is dramatic: the Levite's concubine, mistreated by the men of Gibeah, is at the heart of a national crisis. Over time, the word consistently emphasizes a distinction of social and legal status: the concubine is not the equal of the wife, even if she is the mother of recognized children.
H6370.portee: This word reminds the reader that in the Old Testament, marriage was not always a contract of equality, and women could be assigned a lower status. For the Christian, this highlights how the Gospel elevates the dignity of women: in Christ Jesus, there is no distinction between this one and that one (Galatians 3:28). The biblical text never values the status of concubine but reports it as it was; it is an invitation to recognize how Christ has transformed the Christian view of marriage and equality.

sens: Abundant fat deposit on the body, particularly at the flanks
Manifest and unsightly state of overweight
H6371.detail:
1. The word refers to fat that accumulates excessively on a person's body, especially around the flanks (the sides of the abdomen). In Job 15:27, the prophet Eliphaz describes the wicked man: "His flanks are laden with fat," which literally translates to an abundant fat that is visible and spreads out.
2. Figuratively, this word paints a physical portrait that betrays a life of laziness, without discipline, turned towards softness and indulgence. Excess fat symbolizes a departure from wisdom and the fear of God.
H6371.origine: The Hebrew word pimah comes from a root that evokes what overflows, what exceeds the measure. It is formed to express the idea not of normal fat, but of superfluous fat, that which is added without restraint. It is a rare word in the Bible, emphasizing by its specialized character the excess rather than the mere presence of fat.
H6371.emploi: This word appears only once in Job 15:27, in a description of the wicked painted by Eliphaz. It is part of the moral portrait of a man whom the prophet judges guilty and doomed to punishment: face covered with fat, flanks laden with excess. This physical accumulation expresses a moral degeneration — prosperity without wisdom, self-satisfaction without fear of God.
H6371.portee: This term reminds us that the Bible does not separate the body from the soul: the physical state and the spiritual state of a person reflect one another. Excess fat here symbolizes a life without self-control, distant from God. For the reader, it is an invitation to cultivate sobriety and discipline, not out of vanity, but as a fruit of a life anchored in God.

sens: Grandson of Aaron and son of Eleazar, priest of ancient Israel
He who, through his religious zeal, stopped God's judgment on the people
Figure of dedication to God's justice
H6372G.detail:
1. Phinehas is a key figure in the priestly genealogy of Israel: he is the son of Eleazar, who is himself the son of Aaron the high priest. He was born during the wilderness period after the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 6:25) and belongs to the tribe of Levi. His name means "mouth of bronze," evoking strength and authority.

2. He is best known for his act of religious zeal: when the people begin to sin with the Moabites and worship their gods, God sends a plague. Phinehas kills the Israelite prince Zimri and the Moabite woman with whom he sins, which immediately stops the plague (Numbers 25:7-8). God then promises him "an everlasting covenant of peace" and "a perpetual priesthood" for his house (Numbers 25:11-13).

3. Phinehas then fulfills important roles: he accompanies Moses to war against the Midianites (Numbers 31:6), leads a delegation to resolve a conflict between tribes (Joshua 22), and remains a respected figure in the Israelite priesthood from which the high priests descend (1 Chronicles 6:4-50).
H6372G.origine: The name Phinehas (פִּינְחָס) literally means "mouth of bronze," a powerful image suggesting strength, authority, and steadfastness. This etymology reflects the character of this figure: his unwavering zeal for divine justice. He represents the branch of Eleazar in the priestly lineage of Aaron, making him an important ancestor of the priests of Israel.
H6372G.emploi: Phinehas is mentioned 16 times in the Bible, primarily in the books of Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, and Chronicles. He first appears as a genealogical name (Exodus 6:25), but becomes a central figure during the incident at Peor (Numbers 25), where his zeal saves Israel from destruction. After this event, he exercises priestly authority: he negotiates on behalf of the people to avoid a civil war (Joshua 22:30-32) and is recognized as a representative of God. Chronicles regularly place him in the genealogy of the high priests, highlighting his legitimate descent and lasting place in the Temple worship.
H6372G.portee: Phinehas embodies the righteous zeal for God's holiness: not blind violence, but decisive action in response to flagrant sin that threatens the community. His story teaches that sincere dedication to divine justice is recognized and rewarded by God. It also reminds us that personal faithfulness has lasting consequences: the promise of a lasting priestly lineage shows how God honors those who defend His honor with integrity.

sens: priest, son of Eli during the united monarchy in Israel
man living in the time of the sanctuary at Shiloh
H6372H.detail: Phinehas is an Israelite priest, one of the two sons of the high priest Eli. He served at the sanctuary of Shiloh with his brother Hophni, and both are mentioned together in the accounts of the first book of Samuel as priests offering sacrifices to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:3). Phinehas was married and the father of a son; his wife was pregnant when she learned of his death and that of her father-in-law in battle against the Philistines, and she gave birth in distress upon receiving this news (1 Samuel 4:19). He and his brother died on the same day, fulfilling the word of the Lord to Eli (1 Samuel 2:34 and 4:11).
H6372H.origine: The name literally means "mouth of copper" in Hebrew, an image perhaps of firmness or courage. Three characters bear this name in the Old Testament: this Phinehas son of Eli, another Phinehas son of the high priest Eleazar and grandson of Aaron (whose faithfulness to the Lord turned away a plague from Israel and earned him the promise of an eternal priesthood), and a third Phinehas who assisted Ezra.
H6372H.emploi: This Phinehas son of Eli is named seven times in the first book of Samuel. He always appears alongside his brother Hophni in the accounts of the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3), and then during the battle against the Philistines where the ark of the covenant was captured (1 Samuel 4). The texts emphasize his death in battle, which occurred on the same day as that of his brother, and the announcement of this death to his pregnant wife. These mentions show how divine judgment on Eli and his house was executed through the death of his two sons in battle.

sens: Father of Eleazar, assistant to the priest during the return from exile
H6372I.detail: Phinehas is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile under Ezra. He is the father of Eleazar, who accompanies him during the solemn weighing of the treasures of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 8:33). Eleazar is presented as a priest, suggesting that Phinehas belongs to an honorable priestly lineage.
H6372I.origine: The name Phinehas literally means "mouth of bronze" in Hebrew. In the Hebrew Bible, this name primarily refers to the grandson of the high priest Aaron, a man known for his zeal for the Lord. The Phinehas of Ezra is likely a distant descendant of this famous ancestor, which would explain why his son Eleazar serves as a priest.
H6372I.emploi: Phinehas appears only once in the Hebrew New Testament, in Ezra 8:33. He is mentioned as the father of Eleazar, a priest who helps carry the treasures of the temple during the return of the exiles to Jerusalem. This Eleazar works closely with Ezra in this official task, highlighting the importance of his priestly lineage.

sens: Chief of the Edomites during the time of the Patriarchs
H6373.detail: Pinon is one of the chiefs of the Edomites, that is, the descendants of Esau. He appears in both lists of the chiefs of the Edomite people, in Genesis 36:41 and in 1 Chronicles 1:52, alongside other chiefs like Oholibamah and Elah.
H6373.origine: The name Pinon means "darkness" or "shadows" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes what is dark. Like many names from the Patriarchal times, it reflects an image or a characteristic, although the exact link to the life of the character escapes us.
H6373.emploi: Pinon is named twice in Scripture: in Genesis 36:41 and in 1 Chronicles 1:52. These two passages are practically identical and list the various chiefs who governed the clans of the Edomite people in ancient times. Pinon thus held a position of responsibility and authority among the neighboring peoples of Israel.

sens: Sharp edge of a weapon or tool
Pointed tip of an object
H6374.detail:
1. The cutting edge is the sharpened edge of a blade or weapon designed to cut. In Psalm 149:6, the "two-edged" sword refers to a combat weapon sharpened on both sides, formidable and effective: the image evokes the power of God's word that divides and judges.
2. The word also more broadly designates any sharp point or projection capable of piercing or wounding. In Isaiah 41:15, the "points" of the threshing sledge are the teeth or projections that allow it to crush the earth and rocks: it is the tool that causes damage, effective by its sharpness.
H6374.origine: This word is a spelling variant of פֵּיָה (pe.yah), which comes from a root evoking the idea of splitting or dividing. The Hebrew word first applies to the physical edge of a blade, before taking on a broader meaning: any protruding, sharpened part capable of piercing or destroying. The family of words includes terms related to cutting, dividing, and destruction.
H6374.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe sharp or pointed aspects of instruments. In Psalm 149:6, it qualifies the divine sword, a formidable weapon of the righteous who praise God; in Isaiah 41:15, it depicts the deadly projections of the sledge that God forges to grind the enemies. In both cases, the emphasis is on destructive effectiveness, the sharpness that wounds or pulverizes.
H6374.portee: These images of the cutting edge and the point remind the reader that the word of God acts with formidable power: it divides, it penetrates, it judges. It leaves nothing intact. It is an invitation to respect the strength of this word and to recognize that God Himself is the artisan of justice, capable of breaking everything that opposes Him.

sens: Who staggers, who wobbles on their legs
Who is struck by weakness, physical failure
Who is overwhelmed, morally discouraged
H6375.detail: 1. The word first describes someone whose legs tremble or buckle, who loses their balance. It is the image of a warrior or one who is afraid and whose knees give way beneath them: in Nahum 2:11, amidst plunder and destruction, "the knees stagger" (literally: move unsteadily), exactly what this word expresses. 2. More broadly, it designates the state of one whose whole body weakens: physical strength abandons them, they can no longer stand or move forward. 3. By extension, the word applies to moral despondency: one who is "faint" in a spiritual sense can no longer find the strength to resist, to fight, or even to hope. In Nahum, it is the disarray of God's enemies in the face of His judgment.
H6375.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of moving in a disorderly manner, of staggering. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe instability and loss of balance — which is why it applies both to trembling legs and to a heart that loses its assurance.
H6375.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Nahum 2:11. It is used in the context of divine judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. As the city is plundered and devastated, the inhabitants are seized with fear and weakness: their hearts are "faint," their knees "stagger." It is the classic biblical image of terror in the face of the power of God acting in judgment.
H6375.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of God — and the terror before His judgment — has a real physical effect on those who become aware of it. For the believer, it illustrates how God's power surpasses mere mental intimidation: it affects the whole being. Conversely, those who refuse to submit to God experience this faintness that precedes their fall.

sens: one of the four rivers of the garden of Eden
H6376.detail: Pishon is the name of one of the four rivers mentioned in the account of the garden of Eden. It surrounds the land of Havilah, a region known for its gold (Genesis 2:11). This river, whose exact course has never been definitively identified, served to delineate and irrigate the area where God placed the garden.
H6376.origine: The name Pishon literally means "abundance" or "increase." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing multiplication and prosperity, which perfectly suited a river irrigating a fertile region rich in precious resources like gold.
H6376.emploi: Pishon is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 2:11, where Moses describes the four great rivers that God used to encircle the garden of Eden. Among these four waterways — Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates — only the Tigris and Euphrates correspond to geographically identifiable rivers in the Middle East. Pishon and Gihon remain rivers whose current location is uncertain, likely due to geological transformations that have occurred over the millennia.

sens: Son of Michah, grandson of Mephibosheth, member of the tribe of Benjamin during the united monarchy
H6377.detail: Pithon is a descendant of Saul mentioned in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. He is the son of Michah and the grandson of Mephibosheth, placing him in the royal lineage of the first king of Israel. His name means "harmless" or "innocent," although his personal life remains largely unknown beyond this genealogical lineage.
H6377.origine: The name Pithon literally means "harmless" or "innocent." It derives from a Hebrew root evoking the absence of guilt or danger.
H6377.emploi: Pithon appears twice in the Scriptures, both in the genealogical lists of the first book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:35 and 1 Chronicles 9:41). These two mentions are practically identical: they summarize the descendants of Michah. Pithon is cited alongside his brothers Melech, Taarea, and Ahaz. These genealogies trace the descent of Saul and show how his family continued to live after the fall of the king.

sens: Small closed container holding a liquid, generally intended for storage or transport
Container of consecrated oil for the anointing of kings and priests
H6378.detail:
1. A flask is a small vase or bottle, narrow and closed, capable of containing and protecting a precious liquid. It is a portable object, which can be held in hand and easily carried. Elisha commands the young prophet: "Take this flask of oil with you, and go to Ramoth in Gilead" (2 Kings 9:1), showing that it can be transported from one place to another.
2. In the Bible, the flask appears mainly as the sacred container holding the anointing oil, intended to mark the beginning of a reign. When Samuel "took a flask of oil, and poured it on Saul's head" (1 Samuel 10:1), this solemn act signified that God was consecrating Saul as king. The oil in the flask thus represents divine anointing, God's choice, and blessing on the one who will be anointed.
H6378.origine: The Hebrew word pakh designates a manufactured object, a small container with thin, well-sealed walls. Its etymology evokes the idea of pressure or containment: a flask contains and holds closed. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of utensils for worship and daily life in Israel.
H6378.emploi: The word pakh appears three times in the Old Testament, all three concerning holy anointing oil. Samuel uses it to anoint Saul as king (1 Samuel 10:1), and Elisha uses this same object to ordain the anointing of Jehu as king of Israel (2 Kings 9:1, 9:3). Each time, the flask contains the oil that symbolizes God's choice and royal consecration. The use is very specialized and religious: the flask never appears for a simple domestic container, always for holy oil.
H6378.portee: The flask of oil evokes the concrete and tangible nature of divine action: God consecrates His kings not only by a word, but by a visible and palpable gesture, the anointing with oil. For the believer, this simple yet meaningful object reminds us that God's will is manifested through real acts, and that receiving a responsibility from God is a serious and sacred reality.

sens: To flow drop by drop or in a stream
To pour slowly from one place to another
H6379.detail:
1. The word describes the action of water that flows gradually, drop by drop or in a thin stream, rather than gushing or rushing violently. In Ezekiel 47:2, the water "flowed" from the right side of the gate, suggesting a steady and continuous flow that naturally emanates from a source.
2. More broadly, the word denotes the movement of a liquid that spills or pours from one place to another — here, the water that flows from the temple to fertilize the land. This image conveys the idea of a blessing that spreads gradually.
H6379.origine: The Hebrew verb pakah is derived from a root that evokes the idea of slow and steady flow. The form used here (Piel) intensifies or activates the action: it emphasizes that the water flows, continuously streaming. It is a relatively rare verb in biblical Hebrew.
H6379.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 47:2. It is part of Ezekiel's prophetic vision of the restored temple, where the water — a symbol of life and divine blessing — flows from the sanctuary. The use of the Piel emphasizes the continuous action: the water does not cease to flow, revealing the inexhaustible source of God's grace.
H6379.portee: This image of the stream of water flowing from the temple invites the reader to meditate on the divine blessing that emanates from the holy place and spreads to invigorate all of creation. For the believer, it symbolizes how God's grace, the source of life, should continuously flow in our existence to transform us and make us fruitful.

sens: Name of a servant of Solomon whose descendants returned from exile
H6380.detail: Pochereth-Hazzebaïm is a man who lived during the time of exile and return. Although this character himself lived long before, his descendants are mentioned as part of those who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel, during the time of the temple and community reconstruction.
H6380.origine: The name literally means "the one who cuts" or "the cutting" (from the Hebrew verb meaning to slice, divide). It was the name of a servant in Solomon's royal household, an honorable position in the king's administration.
H6380.emploi: Pochereth-Hazzebaïm appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in lists of families who returned to Jerusalem after the exile: in Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59. These two passages are nearly identical and list the descendants of the servants of King Solomon who participated in the return under Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. His name is among those who contributed to the restoration of Israel.
H6380.portee: This character illustrates how God preserved a remnant of His people through exile and brought them back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and the community. It is a testimony to God's faithfulness to His promises, even to the servants of former kings.

sens: That which exceeds human understanding or ability
That which is extraordinary, astonishing, out of the ordinary
An act of divine power, miraculous
That which is difficult to understand or accomplish
H6381.detail:
1. That which exceeds human understanding or ability: the word primarily denotes what exceeds our strength, what we cannot do or understand. When Sarah learns that she will have a son at her advanced age, the Lord asks: "Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?" (Genesis 18:14). The impossible for man becomes possible for God.
2. That which is extraordinary, astonishing, out of the ordinary: a wonder is an event, work, or phenomenon that surprises and amazes us by its exceptional nature. When Gideon doubts the presence of the Lord, he says: "Where are all these wonders that our fathers told us about?" (Judges 6:13). These are remarkable facts that are passed down from generation to generation.
3. An act of divine power, miraculous: often applied to God's interventions in history, His surprising works. Job proclaims: "He does great and unsearchable things, Wonders without number" (Job 9:10). This is the realm where only God can act freely.
4. That which is difficult to understand or accomplish: the aspect of incomprehensibility or difficulty. The psalmist asks the Lord: "Open my eyes, that I may see Wonderful things in your law" (Psalms 119:18), suggesting that a deep understanding of God's word requires divine illumination.
H6381.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the basic idea: "to separate," "to be distinct," "to surpass." What is wonderful separates from the common, distinguished by its exceptional and incomparable nature. The word has several grammatical nuances: the simple form (Niphal) expresses the state of what is wonderful, the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the action of setting apart or consecrating (like an offering taken), and the causative form (Hiphil) denotes the act of accomplishing something wonderful. A wonder is always what singularizes, what stands out from the crowd.
H6381.emploi: This word appears 69 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (over 30 occurrences), where it becomes a key term of praise. Believers are invited to proclaim, sing, and meditate on the wonders of God. It is also frequently found in historical books (Exodus, Numbers, Judges) to describe the plagues of Egypt and the miracles in the desert. In the Psalms, it denotes both the acts of divine power of the past ("your wonders in favor of the sons of men," Psalms 107:8) and the perfections inscribed in creation itself: "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalms 139:14). In the wisdom books (Job), the word evokes the vastness and incomprehensibility of divine works.
H6381.portee: For the reader, this word invites recognition that God alone masters the impossible and that our inability to understand or accomplish something is never insurmountable for Him. It is a call to trust, even in seemingly desperate situations. Meditating on the wonders of the Lord — His past acts, creation, His word — nourishes faith and praise, and turns the heart from doubt to worship.

sens: Extraordinary thing that surprises and exceeds human understanding
Powerful act of God showing His judgment or salvation
Thing worthy of admiration and praise
H6382.detail:
1. A prodigy is primarily an extraordinary thing, difficult to understand, that provokes astonishment — something that is out of the ordinary and exceeds what was expected. In Isaiah 9:5, the Messiah Himself is called "Wonderful," showing that His coming is a prodigy, a reality so great that it inspires wonder.
2. In the Bible, this word often designates the powerful action of God: His acts of judgment and deliverance that demonstrate His dominion over the world. Psalm 77:15 says, "You are the God who performs wonders," speaking of the extraordinary actions through which God intervenes in history — like the plagues of Egypt or the crossing of the Red Sea.
3. Finally, a prodigy is what deserves praise and admiration. The heavens "celebrate your wonders" (Psalm 89:6): God's works are so great that they naturally provoke the celebration and acknowledgment of His power.
H6382.origine: The Hebrew word pe.le comes from a root that means "to separate" or "to distinguish," hence the idea of something that stands out, which is remarkable and worthy of notice. It is something that distinguishes itself from the normal course of things. The word belongs to the family of those that express astonishment and admiration in the face of the extraordinary.
H6382.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and the prophets. It is used to celebrate God's powerful actions toward His people: the plagues of Egypt (Psalm 78:12), the leading in the desert, deliverance. The psalmists use it to exhort the people to remember and recount the wonders of God (Psalm 77:12). Isaiah also applies it to God's action in judgment (Isaiah 29:14) and to the coming of the Messiah (Isaiah 9:5). It is a word of praise and acknowledgment.
H6382.portee: The prodigy reminds the believer that God acts in history in a visible and powerful way. Recognizing God's wonders in one's own life and in Scripture is to cultivate wonder and gratitude toward His sovereign action. This strengthens faith by showing that God is not distant, but intervenes to save and judge according to His justice.

sens: That exceeds human understanding, that escapes comprehension
That inspires wonder by its incomprehensible or extraordinary nature
That manifests a superhuman wisdom or perfection
H6383.detail:
1. The word describes what is so extraordinary that it cannot be understood or explained. When the angel of the Lord responds to Manoah that his name is "Wonderful," it means that this name is beyond what a man can conceive or know (Judges 13:18). It is something so great that it escapes our capacity for understanding.
2. The word evokes wonder and admiration in the face of something that surpasses us. God's knowledge is "wonderful": it is so deep and perfect that man cannot fully grasp it, even if he recognizes its beauty and greatness (Psalms 139:6). It is the experience of one who contemplates a reality beyond his reach.
3. More broadly, the word characterizes everything that manifests a wisdom, power, or perfection that can only come from God and that inspires admiration and reverence.
H6383.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of separating, distinguishing, standing out from the ordinary. A "wonderful" name or knowledge is something that radically distinguishes itself from the common, that is set apart, inaccessible. The family of this word shares this notion of what exceeds normal categories.
H6383.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Judges 13:18, the angel of the Lord declares that his name is "Wonderful": he refuses to reveal it because this name belongs to a divine reality that transcends what can be expressed in human words. In Psalms 139:6, David, contemplating God's knowledge, calls it "wonderful," acknowledging that this infinite wisdom completely surpasses him. In both cases, the word emphasizes a fundamental limit: there is in God a reality that escapes human understanding, and this limit inspires admiration rather than frustration.
H6383.portee: This word reminds us that God possesses an infinite depth that our finite minds can never fully grasp. Far from diminishing our faith, this recognition of our limits should fill us with wonder and humility before Him whose ways and thoughts surpass us. It is an invitation to rest in God's wisdom rather than to pretend to understand everything.

sens: descendants of Pallu, a son of Reuben
H6384.detail: The Palluites are the members of the family clan descending from Pallu, the second son of Reuben. During the census of Israel in the desert, Moses records the families of each tribe and specifically mentions "the family of the Palluites" (Numbers 26:5), thus recognizing the genealogical importance of this lineage among the Reubenites.
H6384.origine: The name "Palluites" derives from Pallu (פַּלּוּא), which means "wonderful" or "extraordinary." This patronym follows the usual Hebrew formula for designating a family group: the name of the ancestor to which the suffix -i (or -ites in French) is added, thus forming an ethnic or tribal adjective. Pallu is an ancestor explicitly named in Genesis 46:9 as one of the four sons of Reuben.
H6384.emploi: The term appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:5, during the second census of the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the desert. This passage enumerates all the clans of Reuben to know the number of warriors available before the conquest of Canaan. The mention of the Palluites as an established clan shows that this family had maintained and developed since the time of the Exodus.

sens: To divide into parts, into distinct portions
To open or dig a passage through something
To separate, disunite (people or their words)
H6385.detail:
1. To divide into parts, into distinct portions: the verb describes the action of sharing something among several. This is the meaning of the proper name Peleg in Genesis 10:25: "In his time the earth was divided," suggesting a separation of continents or peoples after the Flood.
2. To open or dig a passage through something: one can also speak of sharing in the sense of making an opening or a path. In Job 38:25, God asks, "Who has opened a passage for the rain?" referring to the channels or fissures through which water flows.
3. To separate, disunite: the verb can be used more abstractly to separate what was united, notably words or community. In Psalms 55:10, the psalmist prays to the Lord to "divide their tongues," meaning to create confusion and misunderstanding among his adversaries, as at Babel.
H6385.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּלַג comes from a root that suggests separation or splitting. The proper name Peleg (פֶּלֶג), which literally means "division" or "stream" (a term that implies a flowing that is separated), derives directly from it. This verb is found in Aramaic in the form פְּלַג (pe.lag), with the same meaning. The basic image is that of splitting or digging a line that separates.
H6385.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 10:25 and 1 Chronicles 1:19 (two parallel verses), it refers to a division on a world scale: the earth was divided in the time of Peleg, probably after the Tower of Babel. In Job 38:25, it refers to the opening of a passage to allow rain to flow. In Psalms 55:10, it takes on a more abstract and combative nuance: to divide the languages of adversaries to prevent them from understanding each other. The verb remains concrete in all cases, even when it applies to immaterial realities like speech.
H6385.portee: This word reminds the reader that the division of the world — geographical, linguistic, or simply among people — is a reality rooted in biblical history since the origins. It also shows that God controls separations: He creates the paths of water, He divides the tongues of the wicked. For the believer, it is an invitation to see in fractures and relational difficulties not an absurdity, but an order stemming from divine will.

sens: To be separated into distinct parts
To be split, broken in its unity
H6386.detail: 1. To be separated into distinct parts: the word describes a sharing, a separation into segments or portions. In the dream of Nebuchadnezzar that Daniel interprets, the future kingdom will be "divided," meaning it will lose its unity and fragment into several parts (Daniel 2:41). 2. To be split, broken in its unity: beyond simple physical separation, the term evokes a rupture of cohesion, a weakness resulting from this fragmentation. The "divided" kingdom may contain iron (strength), but it will be mixed with clay (fragility) and will not hold together.
H6386.origine: The Aramaic word פְּלַג comes from a root that means "to cut" or "to separate." The same meaning is found in biblical Hebrew: the verb evokes the action of dividing something into distinct parts or segments. The image is one of a clear separation, a schism that creates separate elements rather than a coherent whole.
H6386.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:41, at the heart of the interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic dream. Daniel explains that the future kingdom, symbolized by a statue with feet mixed of clay and iron, will be "divided." This prophetic context shows that division signifies not only a physical separation but also a political and military weakness, for unlike pure iron, the mixture of clay and iron cannot form a solid and indestructible empire.
H6386.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that earthly kingdoms and powers that divide lose their strength and stability. It is a lesson on the fragility of empires built on mixed or unstable foundations, implicitly contrasting with the kingdom of God, which Daniel 2 presents as unique, unshakeable, and eternal. This encourages the believer to seek their foundation in the unity of God's people rather than in the powers of the world.

sens: Portion equal to the division of a whole into two parts
Limited duration, segment of time
Fraction or division of a period
H6387.detail:
1. The word designates half, that is, one of the two equal portions when dividing a whole into two. This is the primary and simplest meaning: if something is cut in two, each piece is a half.
2. Applied to time, it designates a limited period, a fraction of duration. In Daniel 7:25, "a time, times, and half a time" describes a period of tribulation: this literally means 3.5 years or 3.5 periods ("a time" = 1 year, "times" = 2 years, "half a time" = 0.5 year). It is a division of time that marks a limit, a predetermined end to the suffering of the saints.
H6387.origine: The Hebrew word פְּלַג (pe.lag) expresses the idea of sharing or division. It comes from a root that suggests the act of splitting, dividing into two distinct parts. This root evokes the concrete image of sharing: when something is divided, it is rendered into two halves. The word belongs to the simple vocabulary of distribution and measurement.
H6387.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in Daniel 7:25. There it designates a fragment of prophetic time. In the context of Daniel's dream, "a time, times, and half a time" is a symbolic or literal duration of 3.5 years (or periods), marking the duration of the persecution of the saints by the little horn. It is a precise and limited use, but it carries major importance in the interpretation of the end times.
H6387.portee: For the believer, this phrase from Daniel 7:25 teaches that even periods of tribulation and persecution are limited in time. God does not allow His saints to be oppressed indefinitely: He knows the duration and has set it. It is a message of hope: suffering has an end, a half that concludes the period of distress. This reinforces trust in divine sovereignty over history.

sens: Small body of water that flows naturally
Flow of water in general
Figurative flow or outpouring
H6388.detail:
1. A stream is a small body of water that flows on the earth: this is the concrete image of the word. In Job 29:6, the poet evokes a time of abundance when "the rock poured out rivers of oil near me," an image of prosperity where even the stone produces streams. In Psalms 1:3, the one who meditates on the law is "like a tree planted by streams of water," which nourishes and causes it to prosper.
2. The word more broadly designates any flow or outpouring of water, whether natural or miraculous. In Psalms 46:5, "there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God," an image of divine protection that flows like a living source. In Psalms 65:10, "the stream of God is full of water," referring to the rain or water from heaven that fertilizes the earth.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to any flow or overflow: in Psalms 119:136, the one who sees injustice "pours out torrents of water" (floods of tears), and in Proverbs 5:16, the "streams" become a metaphor for debauchery that spreads publicly.
H6388.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּלֶג (peleg) belongs to the family of words that express the movement and division of water. It is close to the root meaning "to divide" or "to separate": a stream is what divides and flows. This word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and Wisdom literature, where it often carries a poetic and symbolic charge.
H6388.emploi: The word appears ten times, primarily in the Psalms and wisdom literature. It first designates real streams: those that flowed near Job (Job 29:6), those of the valleys that God irrigates (Psalms 65:10, Isaiah 30:25). But it quickly becomes an image: a stream nourishes the righteous tree (Psalms 1:3); divine currents protect the city of God (Psalms 46:5). It can also designate the flow of tears (Psalms 119:136, Lamentations 3:48) or the overflow of sin (Proverbs 5:16). In Proverbs 21:1, "the heart of the king is a stream of water" that the Lord directs — an image of divine sovereignty over what might seem unavoidable.
H6388.portee: This word reminds the believer that all that flows and nourishes — water, protection, grace — comes from God. It invites one to be "near the stream" (near His word, like the tree in Psalm 1) to be fruitful. It also shows that the human heart, even that of a powerful king, flows in God's hand like a stream. Finally, it unites the concrete and the spiritual: the rain that falls on the field and the tear of repentance hold the same dignity before God.

sens: Patriarchal figure living at the time when the earth was divided
Son of Eber and brother of Joktan
Father of Rehu (in the genealogy of Noah)
H6389.detail: Peleg is a man who appears in the genealogies of Genesis, representing an important step in the lineage that leads from Noah to Abraham. His name means "division" in Hebrew, as he was born at a time when "the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25) — which ancient commentators often interpret as the dispersion and division of peoples that followed the Tower of Babel. Peleg is the son of Eber and the elder brother of Joktan (Genesis 11:16), who himself had several sons and founded several Arab peoples. Peleg became the father of Rehu at the age of thirty (Genesis 11:18), and he lived a total of two hundred thirty-nine years, which is much less than his ancestors Noah or Shem, but more than those who would come after him — a biblical indication that human lifespan was gradually decreasing.
H6389.origine: The Hebrew name פֶּלֶג (Peleg) literally means "division" or "sharing"; it comes from a root denoting the action of dividing or sharing a portion of land. The motif of the name explains its popular etymology in the biblical text itself: "because in his time the earth was divided." His name thus recalls the historical or theological event of the dispersion of peoples.
H6389.emploi: Peleg is mentioned seven times in the Bible, always in genealogical contexts: three times in Genesis (chapters 10 and 11) and four times in Chronicles (chapter 1), where his descendants are listed. Each mention places him in the chain of God's people, from Noah to Abraham. There is no specific action narrative concerning him: he is presented solely as a link in a genealogy, which shows the importance attached to the transmission of divine worship from one generation to the next during the patriarchal period.
H6389.portee: Peleg reminds readers that God maintains a faithful people through the generations, even at the time of the dispersion of peoples following Babel. His existence and lineage show that God's covenant with the line of Shem and Eber persists amid judgment. Knowledge of these genealogies anchors faith in the continuity of the divine plan, which will culminate in Abraham and the promise.

sens: Natural watercourse, smaller than a river
Division, section, or part of a whole
(Figuratively) Abundance, prosperity that flows
H6390.detail:
1. A stream is a small watercourse that flows on the land, narrower and less powerful than a river or torrent. In Job 20:17, the word refers to streams as symbols of wealth and abundance in the image of "honey and milk," evoking a generous and fertile land that brings its natural blessings.
2. The word can also mean a division or section of a whole — a sharing, a distribution into parts. This meaning reflects the idea of the watercourse that divides and spreads.
3. Figuratively, a stream represents the continuous flow of prosperity and blessing. In the context of Job, these are not mere streams of ordinary water, but streams of honey and milk, images of divine abundance.
H6390.origine: The Hebrew word פְּלַגָּה (pelaggah) is related to the root פלג (palag), which means "to divide, share, split." The basic image is that of water dividing and flowing in several directions. This term thus evokes both the idea of physical division and the continuous flow of a source. The notion of a stream brings together both: it is water that flows after having divided.
H6390.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 20:17. It appears in a passage where Zophar describes the wicked who will never enjoy prosperity, contrary to what he believes. The term "stream" occurs in a poetic enumeration of abundant goods — streams, torrents, rivers — to emphasize what the wicked will not possess. The unique use of the word in a context of wealth and abundance shows that the Bible imbues it with strong symbolic value, linked to material blessing and divine generosity.
H6390.portee: This passage reminds the believer that true prosperity and abundance come from God and are linked to righteousness. The image of the stream flowing naturally invites one not to seek to possess or hoard goods greedily, but to recognize that it is God who distributes His blessing. For those who walk in the fear of God, abundance flows freely like a generous stream.

sens: Watercourse or stream that cuts and divides the land
Separation, distinction between groups or categories
Sharing or distribution of a whole into parts
H6391.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a stream or watercourse, as it traces a line that divides the soil: "Near the streams of Reuben" (Judges 5:15-16) evokes the geological formations of the territory of Reuben, marked by these natural divisions of the land.
2. By extension, it describes anything that creates a distinction or separation between groups: in 2 Chronicles 35:5, the text speaks of "different paternal houses," meaning families distributed and classified according to their divisions.
3. The word can also evoke the idea of sharing or distribution: this separation into distinct parts that any organized division implies.
H6391.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to split" or "to divide" — the idea of a cut, a separation. A stream is naturally a division of the land: it cuts it, separates it into portions. Aramaic uses exactly the same word with the same meaning.
H6391.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In the first two uses (Judges 5:15-16), it refers to the streams of Reuben — a description of the territory, where water carves and divides the land. In the third use (2 Chronicles 35:5), it means the divisions of the Levitical families, that is, the distinct and separate groups. The concrete meaning (stream) and the abstract meaning (division, classification) coexist in biblical usage.
H6391.portee: This word reminds us how nature itself — the flowing and dividing water — can serve as a metaphor for the order and organization of God's people. Division is not disorder: it is a structure that allows each one (each family, each group) to find its place and role. For the reader, it is an invitation to see how God organizes His people by distinguishing and distributing them according to wise order.

sens: Organized group within a community
Division of a whole according to an established order
Order or rank assigned to a function
H6392.detail:
1. The word "class" refers to an organized group of people sharing the same function or role. In Ezra 6:18, it speaks of the priests established according to their "classes" — that is, divided into distinct groups, each taking its turn in service at the temple.
2. More broadly, it is a division of a larger whole according to a pre-established order or system. The Levites are also organized according to their "divisions" for the service of God: each group has its place and specific task.
3. The word also carries the idea of order and structure: these classes are not disorderly, but the result of thoughtful organization, inscribed in the books ("as it is written in the book of Moses").
H6392.origine: This Aramaic word derives from a root meaning "to separate" or "to divide." It is close to the Hebrew word of the same form (פְּלֻגָּה) and shares the same basic imagery: taking a whole and dividing it into distinct, ordered, and understandable portions. This root expresses the idea of intentional separation, not chaotic, but organized for a purpose.
H6392.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 6:18. This passage revisits the reorganization of worship after the return from exile. The context is that of the restoration of the temple: the priests and Levites are established "according to their classes" or "divisions," each taking its place in a ritualized and ordered service. This passage shows how Israel, returned from captivity, reconstructs the institutions of worship while respecting the ancient order, that of the "book of Moses." The word thus emphasizes the importance of structure and organization in the service of God.
H6392.portee: This word reminds the reader that the service of God does not arise from chance or improvisation, but from a thoughtful and transmitted order. The organized "classes" of ancient worship teach that God loves order and structure: each has its place, its function, its time. For the Christian today, this invites seeking a certain ordered organization within the Church, where the gifts and roles of each fit into a coherent whole and serve the common good.

sens: The hard and durable metal used to make weapons and tools
Raw material of war and strength
Hardness, unyielding strength
H6393.detail:
1. Iron is the dark gray, very strong and heavy metal that ancient people extracted from ore: men used it to forge swords, spears, war chariots, and tools. In Nahum 2:4, the prophet describes the gleaming chariots whose blades and armor are made of iron — it is the image of irresistible military power shining in the daylight of battle.
2. Iron thus represents brute strength, military power, domination: when speaking of the "iron" that gleams, it refers to the threat of the sword and war. It is a symbol of what crushes and conquers.
3. Figuratively, iron becomes the image of what is hard, inflexible, relentless: a will of iron, a heart of iron. In the Bible, it is the very material of violence and conflict.
H6393.origine: The Hebrew word פְּלָדָה (peladah) has designated iron since ancient Semitic times. It comes from a root related to the idea of hardness and resistance. Iron was precious in ancient times: it was found naturally on earth only very rarely, and the peoples who mastered its production and forging had a decisive military advantage. This is why this metal became the very symbol of power and military domination in biblical imagery.
H6393.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 2:4. The prophet Nahum announces divine judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria: he describes an army charging into attack, with its gleaming iron chariots. It is a terrifying picture of the war machine bearing down on the city. The prophet uses the image of gleaming iron to show both the overwhelming power of the conqueror and the imminence of punishment: the iron glistens, the spears are brandished, the battle is set. This unique usage anchors the word in an apocalyptic context — that of inevitable judgment.
H6393.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that human military power and domination, however brilliant and impressive they may seem, remain tools of judgment in the hands of God. Nahum teaches that even the greatest army cannot withstand divine justice: the gleaming iron is merely the instrument of a higher will. It is a call not to be intimidated by the brute force of the world, but to remember that God alone holds the reins of history.

sens: Son of Nahor and Milcah, younger brother of Abraham
H6394.detail: Pildasch is one of the eight sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother. He is born from the union of Nahor with Milcah, his wife (or his niece according to some traditions). He appears only once in the Bible, listed among Nahor's children in Genesis 22:22, where the text mentions him alongside his brothers Uz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, and Jidlaph. This genealogical statement shows the grounding of the promise made to Abraham: while Abraham, without a son from his wife Sarah, awaits the fulfillment of the divine promise, his brother Nahor already has a numerous offspring.
H6394.origine: The name Pildasch literally means "flame of fire" or "brightness of fire." It combines two elements: a root evoking flame or light, and a word denoting fire or brightness. Although we know of only one occurrence of this name in the Bible, it fits within the tradition of Semitic names from the patriarchal period, which often describe visible qualities or states — here vivacity and intensity. It is a period-typical name among the descendants of Nahor.
H6394.emploi: Pildasch is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 22:22. He is included in the list of children born to Nahor and Milcah after Abraham and Nahor separated in Mesopotamia. This genealogical list aims to show the family ties between Abraham and the peoples surrounding him — Nahor remains in Aram-Naharaim while Abraham journeys toward Canaan. Pildasch, by his name, belongs to the background of the patriarchal lineage, but he plays no active role in the biblical narrative.

sens: Separate, set apart, make distinct
Make a difference between two things or two groups
Be remarkable, stand out by quality
Choose someone for a particular task
H6395.detail:
1. Separate or set apart: the word describes the action of making something distinct, removing it from the common lot. In Exodus 8:18, God "distinguishes" the land of Goshen by setting it apart: there, no flies will torment the Israelites, unlike the rest of Egypt. This establishes a clear boundary between two realities.
2. Make a difference between two groups: this means to treat differently, to establish a separation. In Exodus 9:4, the Lord "distinguishes" the flocks of Israel from the flocks of the Egyptians: nothing will perish among Israel, but the Egyptians will lose theirs. The word emphasizes the contrast intended by God between two peoples.
3. Be remarkable or wonderful: in this sense, the word expresses what stands out from the ordinary by its quality or impressive character. Psalms 139:14 says "I am wonderfully made" (literally "distinguished"), speaking of the creation of man: God shaped him in a remarkable and admirable way.
4. Choose or designate someone: this means to recognize and set apart a person for a special role. In Psalms 4:4, "the Lord has chosen a godly man": he has set him apart from the common lot to make him his privileged servant.
H6395.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of separation and distinction. It is related to the image of sorting or sharing: one "separates" something from others so that it is visible, clear, and noticed. The root expresses the action of "bringing to the forefront" or "making manifest." The word appears in both simple (passive: "to be distinguished") and active forms ("to make a distinction").
H6395.emploi: The verb palah appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the account of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 8-11) and in the Psalms. In Exodus, it describes how God separates Israel from Egypt: he distinguishes the places (Goshen), the flocks, and the peoples themselves, affirming his power and his choice for his people. In Exodus 33:16, Moses asks that the Israelites be "distinguished" from other nations: this distinction is a sign of God's favor. In the Psalms, the word takes on a more admiring or elective flavor: God "chooses" a godly man (Ps 4:4), or one recognizes the "wonderful" works of God (Ps 139:14).
H6395.portee: This word teaches that God never acts randomly: he distinguishes, he chooses, he separates. For Israel, it discovers that its distinction from the nations is not due to its merit, but to divine election. For us, Christian readers, it reminds us that we are "separated from the world" by God's grace, "chosen" in Christ before the foundation of the world. The word also invites us to recognize in every creation the wonderful imprint of the Creator, who has "distinguished" us by his love.

sens: second son of Reuben
family chief in the genealogies of Israel
father of Eliab
H6396.detail:
1. Pallu is a man of the tribe of Reuben, living during the time of Egypt and the Exodus. He first appears in Genesis 46:9 among the sons of Reuben who went down to Egypt with Jacob.
2. Pallu is the eponymous ancestor of a family, the Palluites, whose name is given as a patronymic in Numbers 26:5. His importance lies in the fact that his descendants constitute one of the branches of the people of Israel.
3. Pallu is the father of Eliab, who appears in the genealogies in Numbers 26:8 as a direct descendant. Through him, the lineage of Reuben continues and subdivides in the history of Israel.
H6396.origine: The name Pallu (פַּלּוּא) means "distinguished" or "remarkable" in Hebrew. It likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of separation or distinction. This name was borne by founding ancestors of families in Israel, and his descendants are recorded in the official genealogies of the people.
H6396.emploi: Pallu is mentioned five times in the biblical texts, always in genealogical lists. He appears in Genesis 46:9 and Exodus 6:14 among the sons of Reuben who entered Egypt. The book of Numbers 26:5 mentions him as the ancestor of a recognized family, the Palluites, during the census in the wilderness. His son Eliab is named in Numbers 26:8. Finally, 1 Chronicles 5:3 recounts the genealogy of Reuben. These mentions show that Pallu was an important founding figure in the genealogical structure of Israel.

sens: Inhabitant of a city called Palon, mentioned in the lists of David's warriors
H6397.detail: 1. The term designates a man from Palon, a locality whose exact name and precise location are unknown to us today. Two warriors of this name are among the "Thirty" of David, these elite fighters who followed him: Shammoth and Helet.
H6397.origine: The Hebrew word פְּלוֹנִי (peloni) literally means "a certain" or "someone"; it has crystallized into a place name to designate Palon, of which we do not know the history and exact location. It is a gentilice, that is, a term formed to indicate belonging to a city or region.
H6397.emploi: The term appears three times in the First Book of Chronicles, always to identify two members of David's elite warriors. In 1 Chronicles 11:27 and 11:36, we find the names of two Heletites (Helet being the warrior himself, Palon his city of origin). In 1 Chronicles 27:10, Helet the Palonite is mentioned as commander of the seventh division of the royal army. These passages are part of the administrative and military lists of David's time.

sens: penetrate a body by passing through
divide into pieces
plow the earth by tilling
tear violently
cross through from one side to the other
H6398.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to pierce a body, to transfix it: an arrow that pierces the liver (Proverbs 7:23), or darts that pierce the kidneys (Job 16:13). It is the action of a sharp point forcing passage through an obstacle.
2. The word can also mean to divide something into pieces by cutting: the wild gourds that are cut into pieces to put in the pot (2 Kings 4:39).
3. In the context of working the land, to pierce means to plow, to split the earth with the plow to open and cultivate it (Psalms 141:7).
4. The word also expresses the idea of tearing or violating the integrity of a person or thing, as when the earth "splits" to let out offspring (Job 39:6), where the body of the animal opens naturally.
H6398.origine: The Hebrew root פלח (palah) expresses the fundamental idea of splitting, dividing, opening in two. It has given rise in Hebrew to several words of the same family: פָּלַח describes the action of splitting or piercing, and it is related to the idea of separating, putting into two parts. The basic image is that of an action that crosses and divides.
H6398.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts where it involves crossing, dividing, or splitting. It describes both violent actions (piercing a body with a weapon, piercing with darts) and practical and natural actions (cutting vegetables, plowing, the opening of the body during birth). The context determines whether the action is destructive or productive: to pierce with the intention to harm, or to split the earth to cultivate it.
H6398.portee: This word reminds us that our sufferings, when they pierce us, are not beyond God's sight. It also invites us to see the work of the land, of tilling, as an action that opens and prepares, an image of what God can do in us to make us fruitful.

sens: To serve someone, to fulfill a function for them
To worship, to render religious worship to a deity
To obey with submission and devotion
H6399.detail:
1. To serve primarily means to accomplish a task, to perform a function for someone else: to be at their service, to do what they ask. This is the sense of ordinary service, like that of a civil servant in an administration (Ezra 7:24).

2. The word also refers to the religious act of rendering worship to a deity, showing respect and reverence. In the book of Daniel, the three young men refuse to "serve" the gods of the king (Daniel 3:12, 3:18), which means participating in their worship, honoring them through religious acts.

3. To serve also expresses faithful obedience and devotion to someone or something. When Daniel "serves" his God with perseverance (Daniel 6:16), he combines religious worship with the personal commitment of his entire life to obey God.
H6399.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of bending down, bowing before someone — the physical attitude of one who serves. The basic image is that of the humble submission of the servant before his master. In Aramaic, as in the related Hebrew, the word retains this nuance of respect and reverence, far from being a forced and degrading servitude.
H6399.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the Book of Daniel and once in Ezra, always in contexts of power relations and religious loyalty. The three young men (Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego) use it to affirm their refusal to serve the gods of Babylon and their exclusive loyalty to their own God (Daniel 3:12, 3:14, 3:17, 3:18, 3:28). Daniel also "serves" his God consistently (Daniel 6:16, 6:20). The context always shows a serious issue: to obey God or to obey the king, to worship God or to worship an idol. Nowhere does the word denote simple daily work: it always touches on the deep orientation of the heart and life.
H6399.portee: This word reminds the believer that serving God is not a chore, but the expression of a heart loyalty. The three young men and Daniel show that true fidelity to God requires the courage to refuse to serve other masters, even a powerful king. The word invites the reader to ask: to whom am I truly submissive? Who or what will receive my devotion? Serving God means recognizing His supreme authority over all my life.

sens: action of redeeming, paying the price to free
sum paid to release or compensate
price of life, ransom
H6302.detail:
1. Redemption is the act of paying a sum of money to free someone or something from the obligation that binds it. In Numbers 3:46-51, it refers to redeeming the firstborn of Israel who outnumber the Levites dedicated to the service of the Tabernacle: since all the firstborn belong to God, those who are not Levites must be "redeemed" (that is, freed) by paying a monetary compensation to Aaron and his sons.
2. The term also refers to the sum itself, the price paid for this release. In Numbers 3:48, "the redemption money" is what Moses was to give to Aaron for the children who exceeded the number of the Levites.
3. By extension, it is the price that represents a person's life or the cost of their freedom: by paying this money, one "pays" for someone to no longer be bound by a debt or obligation to God.
H6302.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pay the price" or "to release by payment." It expresses the idea of liberation through an act of exchange: one pays a price to obtain someone's freedom. The same root produces forms that designate the one who redeems (the redeemer, the Goel in Hebrew), the one who pays the price.
H6302.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, exclusively in Numbers 3:46-51, in a very specific context of the Levitical law. Moses must count the firstborn of the sons of Israel and the Levites; the firstborn who exceed the number of the Levites must be redeemed (that is, their families must pay a compensation). Each firstborn belongs to God (cf. Exodus 13:2), but only the Levites are dedicated to His service; therefore, the others must be released from this dedication by paying money. This "redemption" is a legal and religious act, a means to satisfy both the law and grace.
H6302.portee: This word reveals an important dimension of the relationship between God and His people: freedom has a price. Although all the firstborn belong to God, He provides a means of redemption, a possibility of liberation. This image paves the way for the great Christian doctrine of redemption through Christ: every man belongs to God by creation, but Jesus pays the ultimate price (His life) to free us from sin and death. It is a lesson on redemption.
